add.issue.name: xlint: check final newline in .md files

edit.description.md:
## Problem

`check_final_newline` runs only in the `.py` branch of `check_file` in `tools/xlint/xlint.py`. A `.md` file gets exactly one check (space indentation), so a missing final newline in Markdown is invisible to xlint.

Hit live 2026-09-27: an edit silently dropped the trailing newline from `.agents/agent-notes-secretary-3.md`. Three sibling notes files all end with a newline, so it was a regression rather than house style — and xlint reported the file clean.

## Scope

- Apply `check_final_newline` to the `.md` branch, under the existing `--no-final-newline` flag.
- Respect the existing fence/frontmatter exemptions where relevant.

## Acceptance

- A `.md` missing its trailing newline fails; one with it passes.
- `--no-final-newline` disables the check for `.md` as it does for `.py`.
- Repo-wide `xlint $(git ls-files '*.md')` is clean, or every remaining finding is dispositioned.

## Notes

- **ai-ok**: an AI may pick this up and implement it without extensive discussion with the human.
- Related: GBNEWPS (frontmatter + fenced-code exemptions) is already implemented in `ed3d27e` but still sits in Todo — that ticket's status looks stale.
- Adjacent, deliberately *not* in scope: `check_trailing_whitespace` is also language-independent and is `.py`-only today. Worth its own ticket.

add.issue.name: Replace the broken coding subagent (mimo) — evaluate nemotron-3-ultra vs north-mini-code for quality

edit.description.md:
`opencode/mimo-v2.5-free` — the model AGENTS.md assigns to coding via `dispatch coding` — **fails instantly** with an opaque `UnknownError` ("Unexpected server error", ref `err_87964db6`, `err_0ac8beb6`). Tried twice on 2026-09-27, not transient; the process never starts. Coding work had to be run on `opencode/nemotron-3-ultra-free` instead, which worked 3/3.

**The evaluation, per the human (2026-09-27):** compare quality of
- `opencode/nemotron-3-ultra-free` — in effect **very cheap**: generous limits, *not*
  bundled into the same pool as big-pickle (unlike mimo and some others), and not
  in the OpenRouter free pool either. So mimo was effectively a *third* generous pool.
- `openrouter/cohere/north-mini-code:free` — a coding specialist (30B MoE, 3B active,
  256K ctx, quality 24). Currently referenced in 5 agent files: `mechanic.md`,
  `programmer.md`, `overseer.md`, `worker-mimo.md`, `worker-north-mini-code.md`.

**Cost asymmetry to weigh:** north-mini-code sits on the **shared OpenRouter `:free`
pool**, which AGENTS.md says to reserve for models with no console equivalent. When
that daily pool hits zero every `:free` model returns empty and everything looks
broken. nemotron-ultra is on opencode's console gateway with generous limits. So
north-mini-code is not merely pricier in tokens — it is on a failure-prone pool.

**The deciding question is quality, because cheapness wins ties.** Cheapness per run
does not compensate for errors, so: given no meaningful change in quality, a cheaper
model is better. That makes this a quality comparison first and a cost comparison
second, with the pool-reliability difference as the tiebreak.

**Method note:** a real quality comparison needs a task with a known-correct answer
and scored output, not a vibe check. The cursor-reviewer-skill trials in
`/storage/cursor-review-baseline/` are the existing precedent for a scored,
frozen-subject comparison — reuse that shape rather than inventing one.

Also settle `programmer.md`'s model pin (see `WV26JZ2`, `3RVME3H`): it names
`worker-north-mini-code` while AGENTS.md's dispatch table says `worker-mimo`, and
the programmer is supposed to delegate coding to a worker anyway.

add.issue.name: Spec: wide all-tasks priority view (separate tool, reuses taskview's selection layer)

edit.description.md:
Write the spec for the **wide / all-tasks priority view** — a separate tool from the tmux pane. Do NOT build it yet; this ticket is for the spec only, and the spec must go through the normal process (AI-written and labelled, or human-written, per the authorship rule in `doc/development.md`).

**Why it is separate** (human, 2026-09-27): dealing with all tasks at once requires a wider perspective than the current taskview provides, whereas the pane is good for focus. Two renderers, one selection layer. Recorded as Decision 13 in `tools/taskview/SPEC.md`.

**Already built for it — do not rebuild:** `tools/taskview/SPEC.md` R21 requires the
selection and metrics logic to be exposed as pure functions over (state, filter) with no
I/O, precisely so this tool can import them rather than reimplement the rules:
`read_csv`, `select_tasks`, `compute_metrics`. The invariant R25 defines
(`shown + filtered_total` = open tasks not never-showed) is the arithmetic any second
renderer must preserve.

**Likely shape to evaluate in the spec:**
- Reads the same CSV — which is the single authority; the epiq boards, `TASKS.md` and
  `STATUS.md` are all derivatives of it, so this tool does not introduce a fourth source.
- Renders a sortable/editable table rather than a fixed condensed pane, so overall
  priority across *all* projects is visible at once.
- Needs an **unfiltered** view, which is what `/storage/Agents/.taskview.yaml` already
  provides for the pane (`categories: []`, `include_bucket: true`).
- The open question this spec must answer: how much does editing belong in it? The human
  floated "possibly even an editable table to manage the overall priority of all tasks",
  which raises the write path — priority is not currently a CSV field, so this may need a
  schema change (a `priority` column) rather than reusing `importance`. That is a real
  decision, not an implementation detail, and it interacts with the append-only
  last-write-wins model.
- Follow `task-windows` (`/storage/Agents/plans/pending/task-windows.md`) as a possible
  consumer: a task window's pane should show only that project, which depends on this
  work having a clean shared selection layer.

**Context:** the project-specific work this depends on is implemented, gated and
uncommitted as of 2026-09-27 — see `doc/reviews/taskview-2026-09-27-a9ee0a.md`.

add.issue.name: Off-vocabulary categories in tasks.csv: research / ai-docs / personal (#61–#63, #65, #66)

edit.description.md:
Five open tasks carry category values that were never ruled on. All five appeared on 2026-09-27, all from the model-benchmark / codebase-comprehension work, and they are the only rows in the entire store that use them.

| # | category | task |
|---|----------|------|
| 61 | `research` | Model benchmark: widen the episode set |
| 62 | `ai-docs` | Correct library/ai/free-model-tier-list.md |
| 63 | `research` | Model benchmark: set G2–G5 thresholds |
| 65 | `personal` | Codebase comprehension learning process |
| 66 | `personal` | First 45-min comprehension block on mms-frontend |

## Why this needs a ruling, not a cleanup

The category column is the membership axis for project-scoped views (SPEC R4, Decision 8). A category only earns its place if some `.taskview.yaml` can scope to it or a pane can ask for it. `research` and `ai-docs` are neither a project nor a life area — they are *activities*. They name what the task is being done for, not what it is about, and that distinction is exactly what the human's rule turns on: **category = what the work is about, not which repo you are sitting in** (SPEC Decision 17).

The deeper problem is accretion. Nothing rejects a new category value, so the vocabulary grows one task at a time, by whoever happens to be in a session. A column that widens silently stops being a vocabulary. It is the same free-text drift already recorded for tags (`verif` vs `verify`), one level up and slower to notice.

## The specific questions

**#61, #62, #63 — model benchmark.** Three defensible answers, genuinely different:

- `work` — `TASKS.md` files the model benchmark under `### Work`.
- `XLib` — the harness lives at `$XLIB/tools/modelbench/`. Precedent: #56 (taskview project-specific) was labelled `XLib` even though its plan lives in the Agents repo, for exactly this reason.
- `Agents` — the plan is `Agents/plans/model-benchmark.md`, the output is `Agents/library/ai/models/`.

`#56` already set the precedent, so `XLib` is the consistent answer unless the human rules the benchmark is work rather than tooling.

**#65, #66 — codebase comprehension.** Almost certainly the same thing as `Personal Development`, spelled differently — `personal` vs `Personal Development` is the `verif`/`verify` drift again. `Personal Development` is the `TASKS.md` section name and is what #22, #23 and #41 were just labelled with in the 2026-09-27 pass, so these two are the odd ones out.

## Left unchanged on purpose

A live session owns this work. Relabelling under it would be invisible to whoever is mid-task and would make the pane disagree with the plan they are reading. Needs the human's ruling first, then one `taskupdate.py update <id> --category ...` per task.

add.issue.name: /storage/Agents/.taskview.yaml documents three categories that do not exist and omits three that do

edit.description.md:
`/storage/Agents/.taskview.yaml` is the file a future agent reads to learn the category vocabulary. Its comment block currently describes a vocabulary that does not match the data, in both directions.

It says:

> In use but not yet ruled on: XLib, Agents, mms-frontend, Mistlands, MaFE.

After the 2026-09-27 labelling pass:

- `mms-frontend`, `Mistlands`, `MaFE` are in **zero** rows. They never have been in any row.
- `XLib` and `Agents` are in use and correctly listed.
- The three values that *are* in use — `research`, `ai-docs`, `personal` — are not mentioned at all (see the sibling ticket on off-vocabulary categories).

So the list names two real values, three fictional ones, and omits three real ones.

## Why it matters more than it looks

This file is the unfiltered global view's own config, and it is the only place the vocabulary is written down anywhere. A filter file that documents categories which do not exist is worse than one that documents none: an agent reading it to answer "what are the valid categories?" gets a confident wrong answer, and `Mistlands` / `MaFE` read as though someone had already ruled those to be projects.

The real vocabulary after 2026-09-27 is nine values: `work`, `XLib`, `Traveller`, `Agents`, `Maintenance`, `Personal Development`, `Business / Career`, `Hobby`, plus `research` / `ai-docs` / `personal` pending the sibling ticket. Of those, only `XLib` has a project filter file today; `Agents` holds the unfiltered one.

## Scope

Rewriting the comment block only — no YAML key changes, and no behaviour change. The human has asked for the file itself to be left alone for now. Not covered by `E5MH4S2` (the wide all-tasks view), which is a separate tool.

add.issue.name: Agents AGENTS.md: `dispatch coding` routes to a big-pickle-pool worker, and worker-mimo pins a model the console dropped

edit.description.md:
`/storage/Agents/AGENTS.md` contradicts itself on the one rule that exists to protect the main model's quota.

- `:139` — "The main model (big-pickle / nemotron-3-ultra-free) is the primary rate-limit bottleneck — **preserve it by offloading** non-trivial work to subagents."
- `:143` — "**Coding / implementation** → `worker-mimo` (console `opencode/mimo-v2.5-free`). Strong coder; **use for coding by default**."
- `:173`, `:221`, `:247` repeat the `worker-mimo` routing (secretary pattern, programmer role, mechanic role).

`mimo` is **pool 1 — it shares big-pickle's quota** (topology in `/storage/Agents/.agents/shared-notes.md`, "Rate-limit pool topology (2026-09-27)"). So the default coding route spends the quota the line above it says to preserve, and it *is* the default: every dispatched coding task takes it.

**It is also self-refuting in practice.** `:141` tells agents to get the worker from `python3 $XLIB/tools/agent-coord.py dispatch <category>` — and that command's WORKER_MAP (`tools/agent-coord.py:540`) returns **`worker-north-mini-code`**. XLib's own AGENTS.md was already fixed this way (`8cb4daf`, plus the WORKER_MAP fix, both committed). The Agents file is the one left behind: `worker-mimo.md`'s description was already updated ("dispatch coding currently maps to worker-north-mini-code") and its parent doc was not.

**Second, mechanical defect — the pin is stale.** `worker-mimo.md` pins `opencode/mimo-v2.5-free`. `opencode models` (verified 2026-09-27) no longer lists v2.5; it lists **`opencode/mimo-v2.6-flash-free`**. A pin to a model the provider dropped is a dead worker behind a live name — the shared rule already says "ALWAYS verify with `opencode models` before pinning a model ID in an agent file".

**Fix, two parts:**

1. Re-point the four routing lines in `/storage/Agents/AGENTS.md` to `worker-north-mini-code` — or to whatever `9J30DNW` settles — so the doc matches the tool it tells agents to run, and coding stops defaulting into the protected pool.
2. Re-point `worker-mimo.md`'s `model:` to `mimo-v2.6-flash-free`, or delete the agent if nothing routes to it any more. Do not leave a broken pin.

**Related, not duplicate.** `9J30DNW` decides *which model codes best* (mimo fails outright; nemotron-3-ultra vs north-mini-code on quality, with the shared OpenRouter `:free` pool as the cost tiebreak). This ticket is the rule-level contradiction plus a stale pin, and it does not need that comparison settled. If `9J30DNW` picks the worker, part 1 collapses to a one-line edit.

add.issue.name: worker-space-bunny agent — record only; needs a justified reasoning level before it goes near any agent file

edit.description.md:
**This is a record, not a build order.** The human has been testing Space Bunny for a few days and it was unavailable until recently — do not wire it into an agent yet.

`opencode/space-bunny-free` is worth a worker slot for two reasons:

- **Pool 2** — appears fully separate from big-pickle's quota; heavy concurrent use of both has never throttled either. Both pools are worth protecting.
- **The only console model reachable unauthenticated** through the Zen gateway: 7 of the 8 free console models return `403 "OpenCode's free tier can only be used from within OpenCode"`. Evidence in `plans/model-benchmark.md`; Cloudflare also rejects Python `urllib` at that gateway (error 1010) while curl passes, so probe with curl.

The human rates it co-equal with Big Pickle: *"Big Pickle and Space Bunny are special because they check themselves instead of making a guess and running with it."*

**Measured so far:** `library/ai/models/space-bunny.md` — the `invoicer` episode, 3 repeats, grade **`autonomy` ×3** (6–7 turns, 10–13k tokens), ~4× cheaper in tokens and ~10× faster than the model it beat, while grading higher. One episode is not a grade: this is a promising signal, not a licence.

**The open question — the human's to answer: what reasoning level?** They have been running the most expensive setting. That is not a defensible default unless it is *shown* to beat lower settings, so any worker file must carry a **justified** reasoning effort, not the max. `$XLIB/tools/modelbench/` is the harness that could settle it; note also that reasoning models need `--max-tokens ≳ 12288` in an agent loop or they return empty content wearing `finish_reason: length`.

**Current state:** `worker-space-bunny.md` does not exist in either workspace. Filed from the XLib board because this repo holds the only epiq project; the file it would create lives in `/storage/Agents/.opencode/agent/`.

add.issue.comment.md:
Cross-reference: `Q397WZG`. Verifying the routing while preparing it turned up a fact this ticket's cost analysis is missing, and it moves the deciding question.

**`mimo` shares big-pickle's quota.** It is pool 1, same as the main model — so keeping `worker-mimo` as the coding route spends the very quota the dispatch rule exists to protect, which is a different objection from the quality one this ticket weighs. `/storage/Agents/AGENTS.md:139` says to preserve big-pickle by offloading; `:143` then routes coding to a worker that offloads *into* that same pool, at 4 places (`:143`, `:173`, `:221`, `:247`).

Also: `opencode/mimo-v2.5-free` is no longer listed by the console (verified with `opencode models` today; v2.5 gone, `mimo-v2.6-flash-free` present) — a second, independent reason the pin cannot stay, on top of the `UnknownError` recorded above.

Neither point changes *which model codes best*, which is what this ticket decides. But they do mean the status quo has no defence: if the comparison lands on `worker-north-mini-code` the pool problem is solved by the edit, and if it lands on `nemotron-3-ultra` it is solved because that model is a separate pool. There is no outcome of this comparison that leaves `worker-mimo` as the default.

add.issue.name: tasks.csv header declares 5 columns while every new row carries 8 — header-driven readers mis-map silently

edit.description.md:
Found while auditing taskview after the category/tag rollout (2026-09-27).

**The defect.** `~/.local/share/taskview/tasks.csv` carries the *old* header line:

    id,status,title,due_ts,chg_ts

but the schema is 8 columns (`// Schema:` comment line says so) and `ensure_csv` in `tools/taskview/taskupdate.py:20` writes 8 when it creates a file. It no-ops when the file already exists, so the on-disk header never self-heals. Field census of the live file: 63 rows with 5 fields, 48 with 8, 7 with 6, the rest wider (quoted titles containing commas — those parse fine).

**Why it matters.** `taskupdate.py` itself reads *positionally* (`row[5]`, guarded by `len(row) >`), so the tool is correct. The trap is any **header-driven** reader: `csv.DictReader` trusts that line and silently puts `category` under `due_ts` and shifts everything after. That already cost one session a whole table it was building for the human. A quiet wrong answer is worse than a crash.

**Fix options, pick one.**
- Repair the header on open (rewrite the field-name line, and migrate the 5-field rows to 8 so the file stops being mixed-format).
- Or drop the header line entirely and treat position 5-8 as optional — the readers already guard with `len(row) >`.
- Or leave the data alone and add a `taskupdate.py migrate` that reports the mixed format without writing.

**Definition of done.** A reader built on the header agrees with a positional reader for every id in the file, and there is a test that fails on the current file. Needs a spec line + tests per `XLib/doc/development.md` — taskview is committed (`250aaf1`), so this is real code, not scratch.

Related: the `tasks.csv` duplication between taskview and this board is `JM8GVW8`; vocabulary drift in the same file is `SNXBR23`.

add.issue.name: taskupdate.py: add `show <id>` — there is no lookup, so a task can only be found by reading the CSV

edit.description.md:
Found 2026-09-27, from the human: *"Referring to tasks by ID is convenient, but I don't have a quick reference right now."*

**The gap.** `taskupdate.py` has `add`, `update`, `done`, `cancel` — and **no lookup**. To answer "what is #40?" or "what is still open in `work`?" an agent has to open `~/.local/share/taskview/tasks.csv` and parse it by hand. The parsing is where `AQQNPAN` bites: hand-rolled readers get the columns wrong, silently.

**Proposed.** `taskupdate.py show <id>` printing the last row for that id as `id / status / title / due / category / tags / importance`, plus `--field <name>` for one value (an agent that wants just the category should not have to screen-scrape). `show` with no id, or `show --category work`, can list the open set — but keep that minimal; the *wide* multi-axis view is `E5MH4S2` and this must not grow into a second one.

Roughly five lines against the existing positional reader. Also worth taking in the same change: a `taskupdate.py list` that prints `id` first, so the CSV never has to be read raw.

**Definition of done.** `show` on a known id, on an unknown id (non-zero exit, clear message), and on an id whose rows are mixed-width (5-field and 8-field history) — all correct, with tests. Spec line + tests per `XLib/doc/development.md`.

This is the piece that makes `AQQNPAN` and the pane-id ticket (`#` rendering) worth having: ids are only useful as references if something can resolve them.

add.issue.name: taskview pane shows no task id — a task can only be named by its truncated title

edit.description.md:
Found 2026-09-27, from the human: *"Referring to tasks by ID is convenient, but I don't have a quick reference right now."*

**The gap.** The tmux task pane renders title only — `truncate(current['title'], width - 2)` at `tools/taskview/taskview.py:371` for the current task, `:389` for the UPCOMING list. No id appears anywhere, so the pane cannot answer "which one is this?" Two titles sharing a first few words are indistinguishable, and truncated titles are worse.

Concrete symptom from this session: asked whether `#40` was the task about part switching, the only handle available was the number — the title had been truncated out of recognition.

**Proposed.** Prefix the id in both places, `#<id> ` before the title, and widen the truncation budget by the prefix width so the title does not get shorter. Formatting lives in the render layer, so this is presentation, not data.

**Half of a pair — read with `EY72YA9`.** Showing an id creates references, and right now resolving one means reading the CSV by hand, which is the exact failure mode `AQQNPAN` describes. Land the lookup (`EY72YA9`) with this, not after: an id in the pane that nothing can resolve is a worse gap than no id at all. The id prefix is nearly free on its own; the pair is what removes the "no quick reference" problem.

add.issue.name: epiq state branch has never been pushed; agent events sit uncommitted and every cross-process sync is skipped

edit.description.md:
**The remote is not the problem — the sync path never runs.** Everything on this board exists on one machine only.

**Verified 2026-09-27:**

- epiq pushes the state branch to `origin` (hardcoded in the package), i.e. XLib's own remote `git@github.com:Xonok/XLib.git`. `git push --dry-run origin __epiq_state__` → `* [new branch] __epiq_state__ -> __epiq_state__`. Auth and write access are fine.
- `git ls-remote origin` lists **only** `refs/heads/master`. `__epiq_state__` has never been pushed. There is no remote copy of any ticket, comment or event in this project.
- Local state branch head is `cef330e`, dated **2026-09-26 21:08**. Nothing since has been committed.
- `epiq_sync` from an MCP session returns `skipped: true` every time (4 attempts today). `.epiq/log/epiq.log` has the reason once: `Skipping sync: the state worktree is held by sync (pid 1279 on Dreamer, started 2026-09-27T11:24:42.470Z)`. The TUI's autosync re-takes the lock on a ~10 s cycle, so a one-shot sync from another process loses the race.
- The log's only other message, thousands of times: `[sync] no own event file changes to commit`. **Sync commits only the calling actor's own event file.** The TUI (actor `xonok`) has nothing of its own to commit, so it never creates a commit — and a commit is the precondition for a push.

**Live consequence.** `Q397WZG`, `DY56JS1` and the `9J30DNW` comment exist **only** in `.epiq/events/g3eadtng57jjeep7b2c7fasva7~pending.jsonl` (22 KB, mtime 14:43) inside the state worktree at `/home/xonok/.epiq-global/worktrees/01M3BVECGNWADVFNJ4311DGPGH/`. Uncommitted, unpushed. If that worktree is pruned or reinstalled, they are gone.

**Options (all need the human — a push is a git change, and the lock holder is their TUI):**

1. Quit the epiq TUI (pid 1279) so nothing competes for the lock, then run one sync from an MCP session. The first real commit also triggers the first push (`-u origin __epiq_state__`), fixing the missing remote in the same action. Not verified from here: I will not kill the human's live TUI.
2. `:sync` inside the TUI does **not** work around this — per the mechanism above it only commits `xonok`'s own event file.
3. Longer term this is a design hole worth reporting upstream: a per-actor commit rule means any actor that never syncs itself silently loses its writes. A "commit all pending event files" path, or a documented `own`-actor override, would remove the failure mode.

Three `epiq-mcp` processes are alive alongside the TUI (4h48m, 18h13m and ~5m old), so lock contention has more than one possible source.

add.issue.name: xlint: flag absolute system paths in tracked Markdown — a tracked file that syncs between machines must not name one machine's layout

edit.description.md:
Raised by the human 2026-09-27 after a path sweep of the Agents workspace: *"As always, tracked files should not contain full system paths."* The rule had no written home and no mechanical check, so it kept slipping — 20 occurrences across 6 tracked files before this was cleaned by hand.

**Why it matters, twice over.** A tracked file is versioned *and* synced between machines, so an absolute path is wrong in the ordinary way (it means nothing on Dreamer, gab, Xena or the LXC) and in the git way (it records one machine's layout as if it were the project's). The designated home already exists: `.agents/machine-info.md` is git-ignored *precisely* so it can hold machine-specific facts. That makes this a layering rule with a known landing place, not a matter of taste.

**Proposed check.** In the `.md` branch, flag a path-like token that starts with `/storage/`, `/home/<user>/`, `/root/`, or `~/`. Message should name the file, the line, and the landing place: *point at `.agents/machine-info.md`, or make the path repo-relative.*

**Exemptions to design for, each with a reason** — a naive check would fire on all of these:

- `.agents/machine-info.md` itself, and anything git-ignored. It is the destination, not a violation. Detection has to be "is this file tracked", not "is it a `.md`".
- `AGENTS.md` setup walkthrough — `ln -s /path/to/XLib/tools …` and an `scp -r /storage/Agents/ …` example. The machine path is the *content* there.
- Plans that describe **another** machine's layout. `plans/remote-opencode-lxc.md` is six `/root/...` paths on the LXC host, and naming them is the document's subject.
- Paths quoted as **evidence**. A model-benchmark row quotes `/home/user/project/relative/path.py` — a fictional path a model copied verbatim, cited as proof of harness defect E9. It describes no real location.

That last pair is the honest hard part: the check cannot be "contains a slash-heavy token", it has to be a deliberate judgement about whether the path is *about* something or *about where something is*. Worth writing the exemptions into the spec rather than discovering them as false positives later.

**Process.** An xlint rule gets a plan doc under `XLib/doc/plans/` and tests, like the frontmatter/fence rule — see `GBNEWPS` for the shape and `XLib/doc/plans/xlint-frontmatter-fence-skip.md`. Same file and same one-deep `.md` branch as `GBNEWPS` and `PMRBFR3`; all three should be implemented together or at least not conflict.

Suggested spec line for the rule itself, if the human wants the convention written down as well as enforced — one line in `AGENTS.md`: *tracked files name paths relative to a repo, or point at `.agents/machine-info.md` for machine locations.* The check catches the symptom; the line explains it to the agent that writes the next file.

add.issue.comment.md: Third rule for the same one-deep `.md` branch — filed as `7HP67R2` (flag absolute system paths in tracked Markdown). Recording the overlap here so whoever implements one of them knows the others exist: `GBNEWPS` and `PMRBFR3` both change the `.md` branch's line-scanning, and `7HP67R2` adds a per-line token check on top. All three touch `xlint/xlint.py` in the same function, so they want one implementation session or a deliberate order, not three parallel ones.

**A second, distinct fence bug found while converting notes to tabs (2026-09-27) — indented fences are not recognised at all.** In `xlint/xlint.py` `_fence_exempt`, the `line[0].isspace()` branch runs *before* the fence-character test and `continue`s without setting `in_fence`. So a code fence nested inside a list item (the normal way to write one — ```` ```sh ```` indented under a `- ` or `1. ` item) never opens fence state, its contents are treated as ordinary Markdown, and every space-indented line inside it is flagged. The closing fence is indented too, so state never recovers either.

Consequence worth stating plainly: for such a file **lint-clean is unachievable without editing the inside of a code block** — you either convert code-block content to tabs, or leave the violations. That is the choice I had to make in `agent-notes-a4.md`, where a ```` ```sh ```` COSMIC install block sits inside an ordered list item; I converted its continuation lines to tabs (shell continuation lines under `| \`, so nothing functional changed) and would rather the linter had exempted them.

The fix is the same shape as this ticket's, just applied after stripping the indent: test `line.lstrip()` for the fence characters rather than `line[0]`. Worth covering both cases in one implementation — a fence at column 0 and a fence nested in a list — plus a test with an indented fence whose body is space-indented, which fails today.

add.issue.name: oc-agent: stop allocating its own agent number — take the name from agent-coord and render it everywhere (title, ports, env, board identity)

edit.description.md:
**Problem.** Agent names come from two independent allocators, so the name the human sees can disagree with the name the agent works under. `oc-agent` picks its own instance number by `mkdir` probing `/tmp/oc-agent/$AGENT/$AGENT.$N` (lines 9–21) and uses it for the terminal title and the port file; `agent-coord.py` allocates `workspace/role-N` separately in `ids.json`, keyed by pid, recycled by `recycle_dead_slots`. Nothing ties the two together — the tab can say `secretary-3` while the notes file is `agent-notes-secretary-5.md`. The human hit exactly that mismatch on 2026-09-29.

**The human's direction (2026-09-29):** "We already have a mechanism for giving names to agents, the same mechanism should be used for as many things as is reasonable." The mechanism is agent-coord (`workspace/role-N` via `OPENCODE_AGENT_ROLE`). oc-agent must consume that name, not mint its own, and it should be rendered everywhere from one source:

1. **Move `~/.local/bin/oc-agent` (machine-local, untracked, 79 lines of bash) into `tools/oc-agent`** — the human's ruling: anything relating to oc-agent is XLib work. Tracked, so every machine gets the same allocator and the same title/port/env behavior.
2. **oc-agent takes its identity from agent-coord** (`coord id`) instead of allocating `$N` itself: same `role`, same `N`, same workspace for (a) the terminal title (lines 24–25), (b) the port-file `role` field (line 59), (c) `OPENCODE_AGENT_ROLE` (line 27 — feeds `ctx` and agent-coord).
3. **The board identity derives from the same role, not from a manual `/rename`.** epiq identities are `opencode/<role>` (e.g. `opencode/secretary`); an agent announces that name and the window already carries it because oc-agent set the title from the same role at launch. No `/rename` prompt should ever be needed.
4. Keep the `~/.opencode/ports/*.json` behavior — watchers (skynet etc.) read it. `OPENCODE_DISABLE_TERMINAL_TITLE=1` stays so opencode doesn't overwrite the title.

**Open question for the human when implementing:** precedence — agent-coord already honours an `OPENCODE_AGENT_ID` override; confirm the allocator lives in agent-coord and oc-agent only renders (per the human's framing, yes).

add.issue.name: Agent notes: bind the note file to the canonical id at session start, and make look-through → promote → clear the enforced protocol

edit.description.md:
**Problem.** Two failures the human named on 2026-09-29:

1. **The note file is claimed unreliably.** Nothing creates or locks the *instance* note file at session start; `coord instance-note` only prints a path derived from the id. Instance numbers come from two independent allocators (agent-coord's `ids.json` vs oc-agent's own), so the number shown in the tab and the number in the notes file an agent actually writes can disagree (see the oc-agent ticket for that side).
2. **Instance notes become biographies.** The intended lifecycle — look through the instance notes, persist what is important, then clear the file — is only a convention in `doc/plans/agent-coord-role-notes.md` ("Discarded on /new unless agent promotes"), so files grow unbounded and the next session inherits every past session's context. The human's ruling: at the **start of every session**, look through the instance note file, persist the important things (promote to `role-notes-<role>.md` / `shared-notes.md` / `HISTORY.md`), then **clear the file** — instance notes stay focused on the current task.

**Scoped work (implementer to refine with the human):**

1. Fix the allocator so the note filename always matches the id the window shows — one source of truth (the oc-agent ticket ships that).
2. Mechanize the session-start protocol instead of relying on convention: a `coord` entry point that stamps a session header on the instance note at start, and makes the previous session's look-through+clear a visible, required step — e.g. the command exits nonzero with a reminder until the stale content is promoted and the file cleared. **No silent truncation**: clearing must be the agent's explicit, after-reading act; the tool can require it, it must not do it.
3. Make promotion cheap: `coord role-claim role-notes-<role>` already exists; a one-shot "promote my instance notes into the role notes" helper turns the look-through into a command.
4. Update `AGENTS.md` (both workspaces): "read your notes before starting later sessions" becomes the concrete look-through → promote → clear protocol above.
5. Refresh `doc/plans/agent-coord-role-notes.md`: it still documents the dead `a1..a8` slot format and predates the role-N implementation; its lifecycle section must state the human's start-of-session ruling.

**Related:** the timestamped human-conversation log (R87HJJN) is a different deliverable but shares this notes-discipline thread.

## Current state (verified 2026-09-29) — sync works

The state branch is now pushed and syncing automatically. Verified against git, not the log:

## The remaining design hole (why this ticket is still open)

**Sync commits only the calling actor's own event file.** An actor's new events accumulate in `g3eadtng…~pending.jsonl` / `…~pending.jsonl` until *that actor's own process* wins the sync lock and runs a tick:

- TUI (actor `xonok`): autosync on a ~10 s cycle → the human's writes flush quickly. Confirmed working today.
- MCP (actored per contributor): writes flush when a lock-winning sync happens to run (the 11:08 commit carried the secretary actor's pending events). **Risk.** Events are only lost if a worktree is pruned or reinstalled while an actor's pending events sit unmerged. Not happening today, but it is the same failure mode that stranded everything on 09-27, and it is invisible until it bites.

Original findings 2026-09-27: state branch had never been pushed (`git ls-remote origin` listed only `master`); `epiq_sync` from MCP returned `skipped: true` every time because the TUI autosync held the lock on a ~10 s cycle; the log's only content was `[sync] no own event file changes to commit`. All resolved: the stale lock (`sync (pid 1279 on Dreamer)`) was broken 09-28 05:12 and the first real push landed 09-27 16:17.

## Options (need the human — a sync-mechanism change to the epiq package, or a workaround)

1. Report upstream: a "commit all pending event files" sync path, or a documented `own`-actor override. Removes the silent-loss failure mode entirely.
2. Accept the current behaviour: each actor's events flush whenever that actor's process syncs, and a worktree prune is the only loss scenario. Document that risk so nobody treats `~pending.jsonl` as durable.
3. If the MCP's event flush rate ever matters, an explicit sync on MCP write (when the lock is free) would make MCP events as current as TUI events.

add.issue.name: bbprs.py: blocks_the_human() ignores `state`, so a PR where the human requested changes still reports BLOCKED ON YOU

edit.description.md:
## Symptom

`bbprs.py` reports a colleague's PR as `BLOCKED ON YOU`, and `--check` exits 1,
even after the human has **requested changes** on it. Confirmed 2026-09-30 on
`mms-frontend` #79 `profile_subscription`.

The human set `changes_requested` at 07:23 UTC. The tool still reported
`BLOCKED ON YOU` on a re-run at 07:23+ and again on a later run.

This is the **inverse of the truth**. Requesting changes *completes* your review
obligation and hands the ball to the author. The tool reports it as "I might be
blocking them", so it will keep sending the human to a PR that is not waiting on
them — until that PR is approved or declined.

## Root cause

`tools/bbprs/bbprs.py:143-158`

```python
def my_participation(self) -> str | None:
    for p in self.participants:
        if p.get("user", {}).get("nickname") == HUMAN:
            role = p.get("role", "?")
            return f"{role}/{'approved' if p.get('approved') else 'NOT approved'}"
    return None

def blocks_the_human(self) -> bool:
    if self.is_mine or self.draft:
        return False
    part = self.my_participation()
    return part is not None and part.endswith("/NOT approved")
```

`my_participation()` builds its string from the **boolean `approved` only**.
`state` is never read. Bitbucket sets `approved: false` for a
`changes_requested` participant, so "I asked for changes" and "I never looked at
it" produce the identical string `REVIEWER/NOT approved` — and
`blocks_the_human()` cannot tell them apart.

## Why it matters

This is the trap the tool's own README names: *"the trap most likely to make a
tool confidently wrong rather than fail."* It is a false positive on the one
question the tool exists to answer, and it is the kind that trains the human to
ignore a `--check` that genuinely matters. A false negative is at worst a wasted
look; this one is a standing instruction to go review a colleague's PR again.

## Fix

Distinguish the three reviewer states, not two:

- `state == "changes_requested"` → the human has done their part. **Not** blocked
  on them.
- approved → not blocked (already handled).
- neither → genuinely blocked on them.

Surface `state` in `my_participation()` so the rendered output says
`REVIEWER/changes_requested` rather than the misleading `NOT approved` — the

  default question, not a bug. Filed separately only if wanted.

## Symptom

`bbprs.py` reports a colleague's PR as `BLOCKED ON YOU`, and `--check` exits 1,
even after the human has **requested changes** on it. Confirmed 2026-09-30 on
`mms-frontend` #79 `profile_subscription`.

The human set `changes_requested` at 07:23 UTC. The tool still reported
`BLOCKED ON YOU` on a re-run at 07:23+ and again on a later run.

This is the **inverse of the truth**. Requesting changes *completes* your review
obligation and hands the ball to the author. The tool reports it as "I might be
blocking them", so it will keep sending the human to a PR that is not waiting on
them — until that PR is approved or declined.

## Root cause

`tools/bbprs/bbprs.py:143-158`

```python
def my_participation(self) -> str | None:
    for p in self.participants:
        if p.get("user", {}).get("nickname") == HUMAN:
            role = p.get("role", "?")
            return f"{role}/{'approved' if p.get('approved') else 'NOT approved'}"
    return None

def blocks_the_human(self) -> bool:
    if self.is_mine or self.draft:
        return False
    part = self.my_participation()
    return part is not None and part.endswith("/NOT approved")
```

`my_participation()` builds its string from the **boolean `approved` only**.
`state` is never read. Bitbucket sets `approved: false` for a
`changes_requested` participant, so "I asked for changes" and "I never looked at
it" produce the identical string `REVIEWER/NOT approved` — and
`blocks_the_human()` cannot tell them apart.

## Why it matters

This is the trap the tool's own README names: *"the trap most likely to make a
tool confidently wrong rather than fail."* It is a false positive on the one
question the tool exists to answer, and it is the kind that trains the human to
ignore a `--check` that genuinely matters. A false negative is at worst a wasted
look; this one is a standing instruction to go review a colleague's PR again.

## Fix

Distinguish the three reviewer states, not two:

- `state == "changes_requested"` → the human has done their part. **Not** blocked
  on them.
- approved → not blocked (already handled).
- neither → genuinely blocked on them.

Surface `state` in `my_participation()` so the rendered output says
`REVIEWER/changes_requested` rather than the misleading `NOT approved` — the
same field name is already used in `--json`, so the string is a display concern
only.

  first thing that would need one, so the harness is part of the work, not a

add.issue.name: Agent-file tickets on the XLib board can never link to a commit — the work lands in the Agents repo

edit.description.md:
`epiq_issue_stats` on `ERZHM60` reads 0 commits / 0 files, though the change is committed as `d3f9b2b`. Every ticket whose subject matter is an agent file is unlinkable from this board.

Cause: `.opencode/agent/` is a symlink to `/storage/Agents/.opencode/agent` and is listed in XLib's `.gitignore`. Agent files are versioned in the **Agents** repo; this board's state branch lives in **XLib**. One board cannot span two repositories — link-by-reference matches commits reachable from the board's own repo, so an agent-file commit is invisible by construction. Compounding it, the commit subject carried no `ERZHM60` prefix, so it would not have matched even from the right board.

Already true of: `ERZHM60`, `3RVME3H`, `2YTGA0K`, `ACA67BQ`, `XS0KMB9`, `B26XEPM`, `Y2QYZV4`, `8GBDHGN`.

**The second board already exists** — `/storage/Agents/.epiq`, initialised 2026-09-27, board "Agents" (`91RTD68`). So this is not a tooling gap, it is a filing-location problem: agent-file tickets keep getting created on the XLib board.

Options:

1. **File agent-file tickets on the Agents board.** Zero new infrastructure, already half-adopted. Cost: a ticket that spans both repos (e.g. `AGENTS.md` + a role file) has no single home, and the XLib board stops being a complete picture of outstanding work.
2. **Track the agents dir from XLib** (real files instead of a symlink, or a submodule). One board, one link story. Cost: undoes a deliberate split — XLib's `.gitignore` names that path on purpose, and a submodule gives only a pointer commit, so per-ticket linking inside it still would not work.
3. **Enforce the prefix at least.** A pre-commit check in Agents rejecting `.opencode/agent/**` commits whose subject lacks a ref. Cheap, but a ref naming a board that cannot see the commit is worse than no ref — it looks linked and is not. Only worth doing alongside 1 or 2.
4. **Accept it and note it on the board**, so a zero-stats ticket is read as "lives in Agents" rather than "no work happened".

Recommend 1 plus 4: the split is deliberate, the second board is already there, and the failure mode to avoid is a stats-zero ticket that reads as untouched. Which is the human's call — option 2 in particular reverses a decision already written into `.gitignore`.

The recommendation in this ticket was 1 plus 4. The human picked it, and the batch is done — so the `human-input-needed` tag is off.

**What moved, and why.** The rule applied: *a ticket belongs on the board of the repo where its change lands*, because that is the only board whose state branch can see the commit. Sixteen tickets failed that test — eleven edit files versioned in the Agents repo (`.opencode/agent/*.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `plans/`, `library/`, `.taskview.yaml`, `personal/<person>/intent.md`), and none of them could ever have linked a commit.

| Old (this board) | New (Agents) | Subject |
|---|---|---|
| `WV26JZ2` | `652992F` | Pin mechanic/planner/programmer models |
| `3RVME3H` | `MWZ2WRR` | Dispatch contradictions |
| `ERZHM60` | `TV8Z0YR` | Strip orchestration blocks (Done) |

| `Q397WZG` | `G8B6T7V` | Agents `AGENTS.md` dispatch + stale pin |
| `DY56JS1` | `8G7GQ4P` | worker-space-bunny record |
| `9J30DNW` | `P1H7VM4` | Replace the mimo coding worker (In progress) |
| `BGMYH06` | `QFS2E3W` | documentation-principles.md + index row |
| `SFGQD7J` | `0FM62TA` | Tool schema cache write-up (Done) |
| `ZCW3B3Q` | `CAZQ0H9` | opencode `.opencode/commands/` check |
| `QKRW2Z0` | `F4SK0WP` | `.taskview.yaml` category vocabulary |
| `CDNXZV8` | `29VPR6Z` | Rule: AI simplifies on its own |

**One finding that option 1 did not anticipate, and it matters more than the filing rule: epiq cannot *move* a ticket across boards in different repos.** The two boards are two separate epiq projects — different `projectId`, different `__epiq_state__` branch, one per repo. `epiq_issue_move` writes into the repo named by `repoRoot`, and there is no cross-repo parameter. Handing it the Agents swimlane id from this repo would orphan the ticket against a node that does not exist in this log.

So the split is only ever maintained by **close + refile**, not by moving. Consequences worth knowing:

- **Every relocation changes the ref.** All 16 old refs are dead; the table above is the only mapping. A commit or comment citing an old ref does not follow.
- **The old ticket stays readable, forever.** Closing is a tombstone, not a delete — the description and every comment survive, and each carries a pointer to the new ref. Nothing is lost, it is just filed on the wrong board in the archive.
- **The split is convention, not constraint.** Nothing stops the next agent filing an agent-file ticket here, which is how 16 accumulated.

**What is left on this ticket.** Option 1 bought the correct filing; it did not buy enforcement, and option 3 (a pre-commit check) was correctly judged worse on its own — a ref naming a board that cannot see the commit looks linked and is not. The real remaining work is making the *destination* obvious before a ticket is filed, so this does not refill. That is a decision about where the rule lives (`AGENTS.md` in both workspaces is the candidate), not about epiq.

Solution: branch `ym7eshs-drop-rotation-cursor`, one commit, 1 file / 1 deletion. Pushed, not merged.

`ROTATION_CURSOR` gone from `tools/agent-coord.py`. The STATUS.md half of this ticket — the bullet calling `rotation.json` a deletion candidate — is on `WKQ371W` instead: STATUS.md is a whole-file rewrite, and splitting one file across two branches by hunk was not worth the fidelity on a state file.

**Two findings worth more than the ticket.** Both are about how epiq actually links, and both cost me a wrong turn:

1. **The subject format is `<REF> ` — ref, then a space.** Not `REF: `. I committed all seven branches with the git convention `VG87T14: …` and every one read as zero commits. The matcher is literally `subject.toUpperCase().startsWith(ref + " ")`. Reworded with `--amend` and `--force-with-lease`; the bodies are untouched. add.issue.name: Write the epiq board policy and the two-track process into AGENTS.md and doc/development.md

edit.description.md:
The human decided on 2026-09-30: full epiq, and Option A (two tracks). Neither is written down anywhere yet, and `doc/development.md` does not mention epiq at all.

## The policy, as stated

- **Todo** — pending tickets.
- **In progress** — entered when it is clear how to perform them, i.e. when the human ai-oks them.
- **Done** — agents put their own tickets here when they finish.
- **Leaving Done** — the human reviews and approves; only then may an agent merge to master and delete the branch.

Note what this changes against the epiq skill: Done means *finished awaiting approval*, not *merged*, and the merge is the agent's action rather than the human's. The approval gate moves to the review, which is where it belongs if the human is not writing every commit message.

## The two tracks

- **Track 1 — spec pipeline.** Feature work, intent-heavy. Plan → spec (human) → tests → implementation → pass-2 review, per `doc/development.md` as it stands. Pipelined through epiq as separate commits, filed as separate tickets, driven by the human who writes the specs.
- **Track 2 — ticket as spec.** Default. Goal, requirements and decisions live in the ticket description. The implementing agent writes the tests the ticket calls for; the branch diff is the review.

Boundary rule: *if the human would write the spec himself, track 1; if goal, scope and acceptance fit in a ticket description, track 2.*

## Mechanized facts that must go in the rules

1. **The subject format is `<REF> ` — ref then a space.** Not `REF: `. The matcher is `subject.toUpperCase().startsWith(ref + " ")`. I committed seven branches the git way and all seven read as zero commits; the epiq skill never states the separator.
2. **Link-by-reference reads local branches only** (`git log --branches --not <stateBranch>`). A commit needs a local branch; pushing and merging are not required for the link.
3. The git rule changes: agents may create a branch, commit on it, and push. Merge to master and delete the branch require the human's approval, per the lane policy. Amending one's own commit on an unreviewed branch is allowed; rewriting anyone else's, and force-pushing master, are not.
4. `gh` is not installed, so PRs are opened by hand from the push output's URL. Decide whether to install it.

## Also needs a home

- `58MXTGY` is forced by this: agent-file tickets still cannot link from this board, because `.opencode/agent/` is a symlink into the Agents repo. Every future agent-file ticket will read as zero.
- `agent-coord.py` claims vs worktrees: `.agents/` is gitignored, so a new worktree has no `claims.json` and `check-clean` reads the shared index. Claims must resolve to the main checkout before per-ticket worktrees are safe.
- The evaluator is worth a small habit, not a tool: `epiq_issue_stats` per ticket, read before the diff. `selfChurn` and `maxIndentLevels` would have caught the xcsv `peek` regression (`f0b81d0`) at the ticket that caused it.

Left unwritten pending the human's review of the seven open branches, since these are the rules that mandate the pattern those branches demonstrate.

add.issue.comment.md:
Partial resolution of item 4: **gh 2.102.0 is installed** at `/usr/local/bin/gh`, from the official release tarball with its SHA256 checked against the published `checksums.txt`. Installed as a single binary rather than via the apt repo, so no new apt source or keyring was added and removal is one file.

**Not authenticated**, and it cannot be authenticated from an agent session. Two separate reasons, both worth knowing:

- SSH git access (`git@github.com:Xonok/XLib.git`) does not carry over to the API. `gh` needs a token of its own.
- `gh auth login --web` generates a device code and then waits for the human to finish it in a browser. That wait cannot survive here: the shell tool kills the whole process group when the command returns, so the process polling for the token dies before anyone can complete it. Tried twice, codes `A944-A396` and `4B9F-D48B`, both abandoned.

So the remaining step is one command in the human's own terminal: `gh auth login`. It is their credential to grant regardless, and putting it in their hands is the right order.

Until then the seven branches' PRs are opened by hand from the pre-filled URLs in STATUS.md. Nothing is blocked by it — `gh` adds convenience, not capability, and the review surface is the branch diff either way.

| Lanes, what leaves Done, sole authorship, read-stats-before-diff | `AGENTS.md` — new *Working on a ticket* |

Before this, `AGENTS.md` had **zero** mentions of epiq and `doc/development.md` had zero on master. The workflow existed in the untracked tool skill, this ticket's own description, and STATUS.md — which is a state file, not a rules home.

## Item 4 resolved, and the suggestion I made earlier was wrong

I proposed checking the tool's skill into the repo via `epiq_skill_install`. **That would not have worked.** opencode's own path table:

- Project skills: `.opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`
- Global skills: `~/.config/opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`
- External, auto-loaded: `~/.claude/skills/…`, `~/.agents/skills/…`

`~/.claude/skills/` is a **home-level** path. `epiq_skill_install` writes to `.claude/skills/epiq/SKILL.md` inside the repository — so the file would be tracked and synced but **never loaded by opencode**. It would have looked like the fix and been documentation only.

The alternative is `.opencode/skills/epiq/SKILL.md`, which opencode does read at project level — but that is a 14KB fork of a tool-owned file that goes stale on the next epiq upgrade, and `.opencode/` in this repo is already a gitignored symlink farm into the Agents workspace. I did not do it. The human's deviations are named in `AGENTS.md` instead, which is the smaller thing that works; if the sync gap on `~/.claude/skills/` ever matters, that is a separate decision with a real maintenance cost attached.

## Left undone deliberately

`gh` is installed but unauthenticated. SSH does not carry over to the API and the device flow cannot complete from an agent session — the shell kills the process group when the command returns, so the process polling for the token dies first. Two codes were generated and abandoned. The human runs `gh auth login` themselves; until then PRs are opened by hand. add.issue.name: A patches file: durable index from commit → ticket, and the Traveller workflow it has to serve

edit.description.md:
The human's proposal, 2026-10-01, for Space Traveller and — less urgently — a repo-wide patches file. Recorded here because it is a design decision with reasoning that does not belong only in a conversation.

## As stated

- The patches file is **not densely written**: most of what a reader needs is already in epiq, and nothing is ever deleted there, so **a reference to the ticket is enough**.
- It is **updated only when a change reaches master**, and at that point the commit hashes are recorded.
- Patches are **merged to master as they come** — no batching behind a release.
- When the live server is updated, **patch notes are generated from the patches file**.

## The premise is half right, and the wrong half is load-bearing

"Nothing is ever deleted there" is correct: epiq tombstones rather than deletes, and a closed ticket stays readable. But retention is not durability, and this is measurable today:

	139 unsynced events across four ~pending.jsonl files, on this machine only

	committed log : 216 lines
	pending       : 139 lines

`0J8YBYH` — closed and merged today — appears **12 times in a pending file and 0 times in the committed event log**. Six tickets, nine comments, every lane move and that close are all one-machine-local. `epiq_sync` returns `skipped: true` and does not publish them. STATUS.md records this as `AZHG0FK`, closed 2026-09-29 as accepted risk; it is not stale, it is current and it has grown.

**So the argument inverts.** A ref in a commit subject points at a ticket that may exist only on one unsynced machine. The *reference* is the fragile thing, not the payload. What is genuinely durable here is the opposite of what the patches file was proposed to avoid depending on: the commit sha, in git, pushed.

That argues for the file more than the human's own reasoning does — but for a reason worth writing down, because it changes the file's job.

## What this implies for the file's shape

It is a **durable index**, not a summary. The board holds the reasoning; the file holds hashes and refs, in git, where they cannot be lost with a worktree prune. Two rules follow:

- **Generate it, never hand-maintain it.** Written at release time from `git log <prev>..<new> --format='%H %s'`, taking each ref off the subject, then committed. A hand-kept file drifts from git by exactly the amount nobody remembered; a generated one cannot.
- **"Updated only when a change reaches master" is fine as stated, but only because the merge is an agent's step.** Under the lane policy the agent merges, so the agent writes the entry in the same action. If a merge ever happens without the file being written, the guarantee is gone — which argues for deriving it at release rather than at each merge, if Traveller's volume is low.

For release notes to be *sliced* from the file, Traveller needs release boundaries — tags. Their workflow generates notes when the live server is updated, so the slice is `previous-tag..current-tag`.

## XLib probably does not need this

The human's own read, and it holds: XLib releases per library (`xcsv 1_0_0` … `1_1_0`), not repo-wide, and "what shipped" is per-version rather than a single release-notes stream. The use case is a live server updated in place. Worth building in Traveller; filing it here because XLib is where the board and the workflow live.

## Open, needs the human

1. Is the file **per-repo and generated at release**, or **per-merge and hand-maintained**? Above argues for generated.
2. Does Traveller tag releases? Without a boundary the notes cannot be sliced.
3. Does the 139-event pending backlog need fixing before any design leans on the board? `epiq_sync` skipping is the blocker and is not understood yet.

add.issue.name: pre-commit hook: run xlint on staged files, block the commit on a violation

edit.description.md:
## Goal

A git hook that runs xlint before every commit, such that **a linter failure prevents the commit** (human, 2026-10-01).

## Current state (verified 2026-10-01)

- No `core.hooksPath`; `.git/hooks/` holds only the stock `*.sample` files. No pre-commit hook exists, and no tracked file references hooks at all.
- `tools/xlint/xlint.py` takes paths positionally, prints `path:line: rule`, and exits **1** on a violation (probed). That is all a hook needs to gate on.
- xlint is **not** on `PATH`; it must be invoked as `python3 <repo-root>/tools/xlint/xlint.py`.

## Why

Every xlint rule is currently enforced by prose (`AGENTS.md`: the tab rule, "violations are otherwise invisible until someone lints by hand") plus whoever remembers to run it. A rule nothing enforces is a rule that gets broken, and AGENTS.md already says to prefer mechanizing rules over prose. This is the enforcement point for all of them at once.

## The blocker to clear first: 114 pre-existing findings

`python3 tools/xlint/xlint.py $(git ls-files '*.py' '*.md')` exits 1 today — **114 findings across 13 files**:

| file | findings |
|------|----------|
| `tools/taskview/test/test_taskview.py` | 88 |
| `tools/taskview/test/test_taskupdate.py` | 15 |
| `tools/pybundle/test/fixtures/{stdlib,single,collision}/main.py`, `fixtures/{nested/server,alias/main}.py` | 1 each |
| `xlib_legacy/{CSV,Config,dumb_http,frac,websocket}.py` | 1 each |
| `dev/xprod/test/discrete.py` | 1 |

By rule: 74 function-definition-split, 17 double-blank-line, 12 unmerged plain imports, 7 missing final newline, 2 same-module-imported-twice, 2 space-indented.

Two clusters are not debt to fix but debt to scope around:

- The `pybundle` fixtures violate the import rules **deliberately** — they are the input the bundler is tested against. A hook that lints them blocks any commit staging one.
- `tools/taskview/test/test_taskview.py` is the most actively edited file in the repo right now (the open taskview tickets). A whole-file check fails every commit touching it on 88 findings nobody introduced.

So the hook cannot simply be switched on. Choose: clean the debt, add exclusions, or scope the check so pre-existing findings do not block. `Q93KNA9` ("exclusion mechanism for non-project code, deferred until it bites") is this biting.

## Design questions — the actual content

1. **Distribution.** `.git/hooks/` is untracked, so installing is a manual step per clone per machine. Either a tracked hook script plus an installer (`tools/hooks/pre-commit` + `tools/install-hooks.py`), or `core.hooksPath` pointed at a tracked directory. A fresh clone must have one documented command that works.
2. **Scope.** Staged files only (`git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM`, filtered to `.py`/`.md`) is fast and matches "did this commit break it"; whole-repo is slow and lets unrelated debt block unrelated commits. Staged-only still means a pre-existing violation in a file you touched blocks you — see the table.
3. **Partial staging.** A partly-staged file gets linted as the working tree, not as the index. Document it, or lint the staged blob (`git show :file`).
4. **Exit codes.** Confirm xlint cannot exit non-zero for an internal error, or a crash masquerades as a violation and blocks commits for the wrong reason. The hook should say what failed.
5. **`--no-verify` bypasses it.** A guard rail, not a hard gate. Decide whether something unconditional (CI, or `tools/release/`) also runs xlint, so a bypass cannot reach master silently.
6. **Worktrees.** Agents work in `.claude/worktrees/<ref>-<slug>`. Hooks come from the common git dir, so one install covers them — but the hook must resolve the repo root rather than `cwd`, or it mis-targets inside a worktree.
7. **No machine paths.** The hook is a tracked file, so resolve `tools/xlint/xlint.py` relative to the repo root (AGENTS.md paths rule; see `7HP67R2`).

## Acceptance

- Staging a `.py` or `.md` with a violation fails the commit, naming file and line; a clean staged set commits with no noise.
- Works in a worktree as well as the root checkout.
- A fresh clone installs it with the one documented command, written down in one place (AGENTS.md pointers table, or the setup walkthrough).
- The 114 findings are fixed, excluded, or explicitly accepted — and the choice is recorded on this ticket.
- Check `doc/development.md` for whether the hook owes a SPEC line and tests, like other tooling.

## Goal

A git hook that runs xlint before every commit, such that **a linter failure prevents the commit** (human, 2026-10-01).

## Current state (verified 2026-10-01)

- No `core.hooksPath`; `.git/hooks/` holds only the stock `*.sample` files. No pre-commit hook exists, and no tracked file references hooks at all.
- `tools/xlint/xlint.py` takes paths positionally, prints `path:line: rule`, and exits **1** on a violation (probed). That is all a hook needs to gate on.
- xlint is **not** on `PATH`; it must be invoked as `python3 <repo-root>/tools/xlint/xlint.py`.

## Why

Every xlint rule is currently enforced by prose (`AGENTS.md`: the tab rule, "violations are otherwise invisible until someone lints by hand") plus whoever remembers to run it. A rule nothing enforces is a rule that gets broken, and AGENTS.md already says to prefer mechanizing rules over prose. This is the enforcement point for all of them at once.

## The panel is clean because it cannot see most of the repo

The tmux xlint pane runs `xlint --watch .` from the repo root. That reports **clean, exit 0** — while 114 violations exist. Both facts were verified on 2026-10-01.

The cause is two separate pieces of `xlint.py`:

- `is_ignored` (`:28-31`) excludes any path with a component named `test`, plus `__pycache__`, `.git`, `node_modules`, `xlib_legacy`. It is a **component** match, so it catches `tools/taskview/test/`, `tools/pybundle/test/` and `dev/xprod/test/` alike.
- `lint_files` (`:33-42`) applies that filter **only while walking a directory** (`:38-41`). A path named explicitly on the command line is appended unconditionally at `:36`.

So walking `.` skips every `test/` folder, and naming those same files one by one reports them. The distinction is the whole discrepancy:

| invocation | result |
|---|---|
| `xlint .` (the panel) | 0 problems, exit 0 |
| `xlint <tracked files>` | 114 problems, exit 1 |

Every one of the 114 is in a folder the panel never looks at:

| file | findings |
|------|----------|
| `tools/taskview/test/test_taskview.py` | 88 |
| `tools/taskview/test/test_taskupdate.py` | 15 |
| `tools/pybundle/test/fixtures/{stdlib,single,collision}/main.py`, `fixtures/{nested/server,alias/main}.py` | 1 each |
| `xlib_legacy/{CSV,Config,dumb_http,frac,websocket}.py` | 1 each |
| `dev/xprod/test/discrete.py` | 1 |

By rule: 74 function-definition-split, 17 double-blank-line, 12 unmerged plain imports, 7 missing final newline, 2 same-module-imported-twice, 2 space-indented.

## Why this blocks the hook rather than merely annoying it

A hook necessarily names its targets — `xlint $(git diff --cached --name-only …)` — so it takes the explicit-file branch and **bypasses `is_ignored` entirely**. Wiring the hook as described would therefore block commits on all 114, including 103 in the two most actively edited files in the repo, on findings nobody introduced. The exclusion the hook needs is exactly the one the hook's own invocation defeats.

So the exclusion decision is a prerequisite, settled first:

- `tools/pybundle/test/fixtures/*` violate the import rules **deliberately** — they are the input the bundler is tested against. They can only be excluded, never fixed.
- `Q93KNA9` ("exclusion mechanism for non-project code, deferred until it bites") is this biting, and it moves from nice-to-have to hard prerequisite. It should be pulled forward or folded in.
- **Watch `2VD2XZC`.** The exclusion set holds `test`, not `tests`. Five files currently sit in `tests/` folders — `dev/{xconf,xcsv,xschema,xtest}/tests/` — and are therefore linted and clean today. That ticket renames them to `test/`, which silently removes them from linting with no finding ever appearing. A rename ticket should not quietly disable a linter on five files.

## Design questions — the actual content

1. **Distribution.** `.git/hooks/` is untracked, so installing is a manual step per clone per machine. Either a tracked hook script plus an installer (`tools/hooks/pre-commit` + `tools/install-hooks.py`), or `core.hooksPath` pointed at a tracked directory. A fresh clone must have one documented command that works.
2. **Scope, and the ignore asymmetry.** Staged files only (`git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM`, filtered to `.py`/`.md`) is fast and matches "did this commit break it"; whole-repo is slow and lets unrelated debt block unrelated commits. Either way the hook needs an explicit answer on whether `is_ignored` still applies — see above, it does not as written.
3. **Partial staging.** A partly-staged file gets linted as the working tree, not as the index. Document it, or lint the staged blob (`git show :file`).
4. **Exit codes.** Confirm xlint cannot exit non-zero for an internal error, or a crash masquerades as a violation and blocks commits for the wrong reason. The hook should say what failed.
5. **`--no-verify` bypasses it.** A guard rail, not a hard gate. Decide whether something unconditional (CI, or `tools/release/`) also runs xlint, so a bypass cannot reach master silently.
6. **Worktrees.** Agents work in `.claude/worktrees/<ref>-<slug>`. Hooks come from the common git dir, so one install covers them — but the hook must resolve the repo root rather than `cwd`, or it mis-targets inside a worktree.
7. **No machine paths.** The hook is a tracked file, so resolve `tools/xlint/xlint.py` relative to the repo root (AGENTS.md paths rule; see `7HP67R2`).

## Acceptance

- Staging a `.py` or `.md` with a violation fails the commit, naming file and line; a clean staged set commits with no noise.
- A staged file that xlint's own walk would ignore is handled by the decided rule, not by accident — the hook and `xlint .` agree about what is in scope.
- Works in a worktree as well as the root checkout.
- A fresh clone installs it with the one documented command, written down in one place (AGENTS.md pointers table, or the setup walkthrough).
- The 114 findings are fixed, excluded, or explicitly accepted — and the choice is recorded on this ticket.
- Check `doc/development.md` for whether the hook owes a SPEC line and tests, like other tooling.

add.issue.name: Rules: technical explanations must be checkable against the artifact

edit.description.md:
Standing rule for how agents explain technical things to the human. New `doc/style/prose.md` + pointer row in AGENTS.md.

**Why:** the human can read AI prose fine until the topic is technical. Then "what does this do" / "explain the reasoning behind X" comes back as word salad — every word correct, no chain. Cause: the model narrates what code of that shape usually does instead of tracing this code, and drops intermediate states it considers obvious. Nothing is wrong locally, so it reads as plausible.

**Rules to encode:**
1. Cite identifiers — actual names, cited line per claim. Vague prose can't satisfy this; a model visibly breaks instead of bluffing, which is the signal.
2. Offer a trace, not a summary — step through the data showing state at each step. Summaries launder errors.
3. Mark inference separately from what was read.
4. Falsifiable framing — state what happens if X changes, and what assumption the explanation breaks on.

Also record the preference in `.agents/shared-notes.md` (it's not written down anywhere today, so it's re-explained every session), and note that the small workers (lfm-2.5-2.6b, qwen3.8-27b, nemotron-nano-omni-30b) are the wrong dispatch for explanation work.

add.issue.name: Stranded epiq pending events: other actors' writes are never drained, and nothing reports it

edit.description.md:
Stranded epiq events: 39 on the XLib project (mechanic 8, paul 31, both from 2026-09-29) and 5 on the Agents project. Detected 2026-10-01 while investigating why `epiq_sync` returns `skipped: true`.

**Mechanism.** `epiq_sync` only ever commits *the calling actor's own* event log. Each actor writes to `.epiq/events/<actorId>~pending*.jsonl`, and `.epiq/events/.gitignore` (`*~pending*.jsonl`) deliberately never commits those. Draining happens when a process running **as that actor** syncs. An actor whose process has exited therefore never drains: mechanic and paul ran sessions on 2026-09-29 and their writes sat in pending files ever since, with no committed log file for either actor at all.

**Blast radius.** 44 stranded events, of which the load-bearing ones are 3 missing `add.issue` events — `CMGDFZF`, `VTJVHMY`, `QN1N82Y`. A fresh clone gets committed lane-moves, comments and tag-adds referencing tickets whose creation was never committed. Everything else paul touched was created by an actor that did sync, so the inconsistency is confined to those 3.

**Two STATUS.md claims are now false and need correcting:** `0J8YBYH` is 17 in the committed log and 0 in pending (STATUS says 12 and 0); the count is 44, not 139. `AZHG0FK` closed this as accepted risk on 2026-09-29; the orphan-creation finding is a higher severity than that assumed.

**Work:**
1. Drain the stranded files — see the ticket comment for the mechanism and the attribution caveat.
2. Prevention: a check that finds stranded pending events and reports which issues have no committed creation, so this is a loud failure rather than a silent one nobody notices for three days.

add.issue.name: bbprs.py: should a bare PARTICIPANT (commented, no approval rights) count as BLOCKED ON YOU?

edit.description.md:
## The question

`bbprs.py` reports `BLOCKED ON YOU` when the human appears on someone else's
live PR without having approved it. That check does not look at the human's
**role**. A colleague who added the human as a plain `PARTICIPANT` — the
human commented, but holds no approval rights — is reported as waiting on
him.

## The two readings

**It should block** (today's behavior). A participant is on the PR and has
not approved, so the PR is not moving because of him. Same *kind* of signal
as an untouched reviewer.

**It should not block.** Approval authority is what makes someone a
blocker. A commenter cannot approve, so he is never the thing standing
between the PR and merge — telling him he is blocking invites him to
approve a PR he has no rights to approve.

The argument for changing it: it is the *same class* of false positive
`3EEXMRK` just fixed. A tool that over-reports builds a `--check` the human
learns to ignore, and this is the second reason it would lie.

The argument for leaving it: it is a semantics question about the tool's
central question, not a field-reading bug, and `3EEXMRK` deliberately kept
the behavior rather than changing it silently.

## Why it is not already fixed

`3EEXMRK` pinned today's behavior with
`TestBlocksTheHuman.test_participant_blocks` so the choice is visible and
reversible rather than buried in a diff. Nothing depends on the answer: the
predicate is one condition, and the test names it.

## What a fix would look like

Key `blocks_the_human()` on `role == "REVIEWER"` rather than on
"not approved", and update the two tests that currently assert the
participant case.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: PR #21, branch `3eexmrk-bbprs-review-state`, commit `3f2fac7`. All four acceptance criteria met, plus the test harness.

## The actual root cause was one level deeper

The ticket says `state` is never read. True, but not the whole shape of it: `blocks_the_human()` decided by asking whether the **rendered display string** ended in `/NOT approved`:

```python
part = self.my_participation()
return part is not None and part.endswith("/NOT approved")
```

So the boolean was recovered by parsing prose. Adding `state` to that string would have worked by luck, not by construction — any rewording of the label silently changes the tool's answer. The decision now reads the participant record directly (`_my_record()`), and `my_participation()` is only ever rendered.

## A second bug the ticket did not know about

Bitbucket spells "no state" as JSON `null` on some records and the **string** `"null"` on others. The string is truthy, so the obvious fix —

```python
state = record.get("state")
return f"{role}/{state or 'NOT approved'}"
```

— makes an untouched reviewer render as `REVIEWER/null` and, worse, makes
`blocks_the_human()` return **False** for a PR genuinely waiting on the
human. It would have traded one false positive for a false *negative*, and
`--check` would have gone permanently 0. `_review_state()` collapses both
spellings to one absence.

I caught this by mutation rather than by reading: the naive fix passes
every test written from the ticket's description. Reverting the original
code fails 5 tests; the naive fix fails a 6th.

## One thing deliberately not decided

A bare `PARTICIPANT` — the human commented but holds no approval rights —
still reports `BLOCKED ON YOU`, exactly as before. Whether that is right is
a semantics question about the tool's central question, not a field-reading
bug, and this ticket is scoped to the latter. I did not change it silently;
it is pinned by `TestBlocksTheHuman.test_participant_blocks` and filed as
`AMCWKQY` for you to call.

## Tests

24 offline fixture-based tests — the tool's first suite. Fixtures are shaped
like real API responses and go through `parse_pr()`, extracted from
`open_prs()` so they exercise the same mapping the live code does; a test
that hand-builds a `PullRequest` would prove nothing about what the API
sends. Each fixture carries a `_comment` naming the case it pins.

Covered: all four participant shapes from the acceptance criteria, plus
human-absent, colleague-draft, own-PR, the `--check` exit codes in both
directions, and the `--json` field. `--check` still exits 1 when a genuine
blocker rides alongside a `changes_requested` PR — the fix must not turn it
into a permanent 0.

## Unrelated drift found, not touched

`tools/taskview/test/` has ~110 unlinted xlint violations (missing final
newlines, split function definitions, unmerged imports) — tool tests appear
never to have been linted. The three files here are clean. Not fixed here;
worth a ticket if you want tool tests under the linter.

Left in **Done** per this repo's rule (finished, awaiting your review).
Merging and closing are mine to do once you approve.

add.issue.name: xlint's exclusion set skips every directory named `test` — 109 violations in tool tests are invisible, and the house rule for test folder names is the wrong way round

edit.description.md:
## The defect

`tools/xlint/xlint.py:28-31` skips any path with a part named `test`:

```python
def is_ignored(path):
	parts = set(path.parts)
	excluded = {"__pycache__", ".git", "node_modules", "xlib_legacy", "test"}
	return bool(parts & excluded)
```

The other four entries in that set are "not our code" — vendored, generated, or
foreign. `test` is the repo's own test-folder convention: `AGENTS.md` and
`doc/development.md` both rule that a test folder is `test/`, never `tests/`
(rename in progress, `2VD2XZC`). So the exclusion set skips **every test file
in this repository**, and it does so silently — `xlint .` reports zero
violations and exits 0.

## What it hides

`python3 tools/xlint/xlint.py .` → **0 violations**. The same linter pointed
at the files it skipped:

| Directory | Hidden violations |
|---|---|
| `tools/taskview/test/` | 103 |
| `tools/pybundle/test/` | 5 |
| `dev/xprod/test/` | 1 |
| `tools/bbprs/test/` | 0 |
| `tools/skynet/test/` | 0 |
| **total** | **109** |

`test_taskview.py` and `test_taskupdate.py` account for 109 of those between
them: missing final newlines, function definitions split across lines,
unmerged imports, double blank lines.

## The part that makes it a bug rather than a policy

`tests/` — the name the house rules call *wrong* — is **not** in the exclusion
set, so the four libraries still using it (`dev/xconf`, `dev/xcsv`,
`dev/xschema`, `dev/xtest`) are linted today. Renaming them to the correct
`test/` as `2VD2XZC` requires would move all four **out** of lint coverage.
They are clean at present, so nothing breaks on the rename — but the fix for a
style ticket would quietly disable the check for four libraries.

That inversion is the tell: the linter is sensitive to exactly the name the
style rules mandate, and in the wrong direction.

## The decision this needs

Which did the author mean?

- **Skip foreign test data only** — then narrow it to `xlib_legacy/test` (or
  whatever the original target was) instead of the bare name `test`, and the
  109 violations become visible and get fixed.
- **Skip all tests on purpose** — then that is a rule to write down, not a
  set entry to infer, and `AGENTS.md` should say test code is exempt from
  style enforcement. Today it is enforced everywhere except where the rules
  say it applies.

## Knock-on effects worth deciding at the same time

- **`XCKN0AT`** (pre-commit hook running xlint on staged files) inherits this
  verbatim. Whether the hook catches a violation depends on whether it walks
  directories or lints each staged file by path — the same distinction that
  makes this invisible today.
- **`bbprs`** (`3EEXMRK`) was the first tool test written to be lint-clean, and
  it is only clean because it was linted by explicit path. A directory sweep
  or a bare pre-commit hook would not have looked at it.
