edit.description.md:
## Symptom

`bbprs.py` reports a colleague's PR as `BLOCKED ON YOU`, and `--check` exits 1,
even after the human has **requested changes** on it. Confirmed 2026-09-30 on
`mms-frontend` #79 `profile_subscription`.

The human set `changes_requested` at 07:23 UTC. The tool still reported
`BLOCKED ON YOU` on a re-run at 07:23+ and again on a later run.

This is the **inverse of the truth**. Requesting changes *completes* your review
obligation and hands the ball to the author. The tool reports it as "I might be
blocking them", so it will keep sending the human to a PR that is not waiting on
them — until that PR is approved or declined.

## Root cause

`tools/bbprs/bbprs.py:143-158`

```python
def my_participation(self) -> str | None:
    for p in self.participants:
        if p.get("user", {}).get("nickname") == HUMAN:
            role = p.get("role", "?")
            return f"{role}/{'approved' if p.get('approved') else 'NOT approved'}"
    return None

def blocks_the_human(self) -> bool:
    if self.is_mine or self.draft:
        return False
    part = self.my_participation()
    return part is not None and part.endswith("/NOT approved")
```

`my_participation()` builds its string from the **boolean `approved` only**.
`state` is never read. Bitbucket sets `approved: false` for a
`changes_requested` participant, so "I asked for changes" and "I never looked at
it" produce the identical string `REVIEWER/NOT approved` — and
`blocks_the_human()` cannot tell them apart.

The deeper shape: the boolean is recovered by **parsing the display string**.
Adding `state` to that string would work by luck rather than by construction, and
any rewording of the label would silently change the tool's answer. The decision
belongs on the participant record; the string is display only.

## Why it matters

This is the trap the tool's own README names: *"the trap most likely to make a
tool confidently wrong rather than fail."* It is a false positive on the one
question the tool exists to answer, and it is the kind that trains the human to
ignore a `--check` that genuinely matters. A false negative is at worst a wasted
look; this one is a standing instruction to go review a colleague's PR again.

## Fix

Distinguish the three reviewer states, not two:

- `state == "changes_requested"` → the human has done their part. **Not** blocked
  on them.
- approved → not blocked (already handled).
- neither → genuinely blocked on them.

Surface `state` in `my_participation()` so the rendered output says
`REVIEWER/changes_requested` rather than the misleading `NOT approved` — the
same field name is already used in `--json`, so the string is a display concern
only.

## Second defect, folded in 2026-10-01 — a bare PARTICIPANT is not a blocker

Found while verifying the fix against the live API, and folded into this ticket
rather than a separate one per the workflow's rule on tightly-coupled follow-ups.

`blocks_the_human()` never looked at the human's **role**. Bitbucket sets
`role: REVIEWER` only when you are **explicitly added as a reviewer**; anyone
who interacts with a PR otherwise appears as `PARTICIPANT`, and the author always
does. So a bare `PARTICIPANT` for the human means **he commented on a PR he was
never asked to review** — and he holds no approval right on it, so there is no
action of his that could ever clear the flag.

**Instance: `mms-frontend` #71**, "SCSS refactor to latest Dart Sass spec" (author
Raul Taremaa). Three comments from the human on 2026-08-31; never added as a
reviewer; Indrek Pertman and Toomas were, and both had approved. The tool
reported `BLOCKED ON YOU` for the two and a half weeks until it merged — naming
a blocker the human could not unblock.

Across all **225** open and merged PRs in `mms-frontend` and `mms`, the old and
new predicates disagree on that one PR and no other, so the fix is one added
condition: `role == "REVIEWER"`.

## Acceptance

- `bbprs.py --check` exits **0** when the only candidate is a PR where the human
  has requested changes. Regression case: `mms-frontend` #79 as of 2026-09-30.
- Exits 1 when the human is a reviewer with `state=None` and `approved:false`.
- `--json` `my_participation` for #79 reads `REVIEWER/changes_requested`.
- Add a fixture-based test covering all four participant shapes
  (`approved`, `changes_requested`, reviewer-never-participated, participant).
- `bbprs.py` has **no test suite today** — the acceptance criteria above are the
  first thing that would need one, so the harness is part of the work, not a
  follow-up.
- **Added 2026-10-01:** exits 0 for a bare `PARTICIPANT` on someone else's live
  PR — regression case `mms-frontend` #71 — while an untouched `REVIEWER` on the
  same PR still blocks.

## Notes

- **Correction, 2026-09-30.** An earlier version of this ticket said the tool was
  untracked and asked whether the fix should land before or after its first
  commit. **That was wrong** — it was taken from a stale `STATUS.md` line rather
  than checked. `tools/bbprs/{bbprs.py,README.md}` are tracked and committed as
  **`64537b2` "Tool for reading bitbucket PRs", 2026-09-28 12:24, on
  `origin/master`**. So the fix is an ordinary commit against existing history.
- **Withdrawn, 2026-10-01.** A `Solution:` comment on this ticket claimed a second
  bug: that Bitbucket spells "no state" as the *string* `"null"` and that the
  naive fix would have left `--check` permanently 0. **That was asserted before
  it was checked.** Across all 225 PRs, `state` is always JSON `null`. There was
  no second bug, and one test was pinning a case the API does not produce. See
  the follow-up `Solution:` comment.
- Separate, not in this ticket: the tool walks **both** `mms-frontend` and `mms`
  by default, and the human ruled 2026-09-30 that the `mms` repo's PRs do not
  affect them. `--repo mms-frontend` already scopes it, so this is a usage
  default question, not a bug. Filed separately only if wanted.
- Separate, not in this ticket: `AK633QC` — xlint's exclusion set skips every
  directory named `test`, which is this repo's own convention, so 109 violations
  in tool tests are invisible to it. Unrelated to this fix and untouched by it.

add.issue.name: check-clean silently reports `clean` for any file in a worktree — nearest_git skips worktrees because their .git is a file, and it never follows the agent-file symlink either

edit.description.md:
Found 2026-10-01 while answering a question about `check-clean`'s "paths span multiple repos" error. **The guard does not fail loudly on worktree paths — it silently reports `clean` whether or not the file is dirty.** A guard that says "clean" is worse than one that errors, because the error would have been noticed.

## Mechanism

Three facts compose into the bug.

**1. `nearest_git` requires `.git` to be a directory** (`tools/agent-coord.py:791-799`):

```python
def nearest_git(path):
	base = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path))
	while True:
		if os.path.isdir(os.path.join(base, ".git")):
			return base
```

A git **worktree** has `.git` as a *file*, not a directory. So a path inside
`.work/<REF>-<slug>/` walks straight past the worktree root and resolves to the
**parent** repo.

**2. `cmd_check_clean` groups by that, then matches by relative path**
(`:801-825`): it runs `git status` in the resolved repo and compares
`os.path.relpath(p, repo)` against the dirty list. For a worktree path the
relative path is `.work/3EEXMRK-…/tools/bbprs/README.md`, while the parent
repo's status lists `.work/` as a single untracked directory. Nothing matches,
so the result is `clean`.

**3. `claim` and `check_clean` resolve paths differently.** `claim_paths` uses
`os.path.realpath` (`:390`), which **follows symlinks**. `cmd_check_clean` uses
`os.path.abspath` (`:803`), which does **not**. So the two commands can disagree
about which file is meant — and the asymmetry is why the symlink case is silent
too (below).

## Evidence

A file in the worktree was made dirty, then checked both ways:

```
$ printf '\n# scratch\n' >> .work/3EEXMRK-…/tools/bbprs/README.md   # uncommitted
$ python3 tools/agent-coord.py check-clean .work/3EEXMRK-…/tools/bbprs/README.md
clean                     (exit 0)   <-- the file is dirty
$ python3 tools/agent-coord.py check-clean tools/bbprs/README.md
clean                     (exit 0)
```

`git status` in the worktree confirms the edit was real. The guard saw a clean
file that was not clean.

## "paths span multiple repos" — what actually triggers it

Not the agent-file symlinks, though they are what *makes you mix repos*.

```
$ python3 tools/agent-coord.py check-clean tools/bbprs/bbprs.py /storage/Agents/AGENTS.md
paths span multiple repos: /storage/Agents, /storage/GitHub/Fun/XLib   (exit 2)
```

The error needs **two genuinely different repos in one call**. The
`.opencode/agent` symlink does not produce it: because `abspath` does not follow
symlinks, a path under `.opencode/agent/` resolves to **XLib** —

```
.opencode/agent/secretary.md  ->  /storage/GitHub/Fun/XLib
```

which is its own silent failure. `.opencode/agent/` is gitignored in XLib, so
`check-clean` on an agent file matches nothing in XLib's status and always
answers `clean`, while the file actually lives in `/storage/Agents`. Per
`AGENTS.md` the agent files are a shared symlink into the Agents workspace, so
this is a path class agents are told to edit.

## Two records describe this wrongly

- **`STATUS.md`** (Blocked) says: *"`claim` accepts a worktree path, and
  `check_clean` then refuses the same path with 'paths span multiple repos'."*
  The refusal does not happen. What happens is the silent pass above.
- **This session's own `HISTORY.md` and `.agents/shared-notes.md` entries**
  claimed the failure "did not reproduce" and that both path forms "worked".
  True, and misleading: it did not reproduce because `check-clean` was not
  checking. Recorded here rather than quietly fixed, because the correction
  belongs where the wrong claim is.

## Fix direction

Three separable things, smallest first:

1. **`nearest_git` should accept `.git` as a file** — `os.path.exists` rather
   than `os.path.isdir`. Then a worktree path resolves to the worktree, and
   `check-clean` reads the right status. This alone turns the silent pass into a
   correct answer.
2. **Make `claim` and `check_clean` agree on path resolution** — both
   `realpath`, or both `abspath`. As it stands they can name different files for
   the same argument.
3. **Decide what a path inside a symlinked foreign repo should do.** Options:
   treat it as the repo it really lives in and say so, or refuse explicitly with
   the target named. Silently checking the wrong repo is the one option not
   available.

## Why it matters here specifically

The human ruled on 2026-10-01 that epiq work happens in a worktree so the branch
at the root stops mattering. `check-clean` is the mechanism `AGENTS.md` points
at before the first edit: *"run `python3 tools/agent-coord.py check-clean <path>`
— `clean` means proceed, `dirty` means stop"*. Under the new workflow it
answers `clean` unconditionally for exactly the files agents are told to check
before editing, and a second session editing the same file is invisible to it.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: PR #24, merged to master as `b7211a2` (rebase, no merge commit), branch deleted, ticket closed. Human approved the merge on 2026-10-01.

## What landed

**`.gitignore` — `.work/`**, with a comment carrying the mechanism rather than just the entry, because the reason is not obvious from the pattern. A worktree's `.git` is a **file**, so `git add .` neither refuses nor recurses: it stages each worktree as an embedded-repo gitlink. 160 bytes naming one sha, no error, in a repo whose workflow is agents committing exactly those branches.

Verified with the pattern committed, both directions:

```
$ git check-ignore -v .work/scratch/marker
.gitignore:17:.work/    .work/scratch/marker     → ignored
$ git check-ignore -v tools/.worktest/f.py
exit 1                                            → not ignored, correctly scoped
```

**`AGENTS.md` — the rule**, placed next to the branch-per-ticket paragraph because `AGENTS.md` is the file every agent reads, and the convention previously existed only in `.agents/shared-notes.md`, which is gitignored. The gap that let the epiq skill's own "work in a worktree" go unactioned was that the rule lived in the one file a session is least likely to read.

Two things the rule states that a directory could not:

- **The registration is per-clone.** A fresh clone's `.work/` is empty until an agent creates one, so the convention has to be read, not inferred from the directory existing.
- **The epiq skill already said this and it was still not followed** — which is the reason it is now in the rules file rather than in a note.

## Not done here, deliberately

- **The Agents workspace `AGENTS.md` needs the same bullet.** The ruling is about epiq work generally and both repos have boards, but that file lives in the other repo, so per the filing rule it belongs on the **Agents** board. Not filed there by this session — the filing rule is written down but nothing enforces it, and that gap is the open half of `58MXTGY`, so it is better raised once than added to silently. Flagged rather than done.
- **`personal/Xonok/STATUS.md`** carries a Blocked item describing `check-clean` *refusing* worktree paths with "paths span multiple repos". It does not refuse them — it **silently reports `clean` for them**, which is the more dangerous behaviour, because a guard that says `clean` is not noticed. Left alone deliberately: the file has uncommitted changes from a parallel session working `FZDMC84`, and this repo's own history records two agents silently undoing each other's `STATUS.md` writes. Filed as **`8FVW49J`** with the mechanism and evidence instead.

## One housekeeping note

Local `master` is one commit behind `origin/master` and was left that way on purpose. Fast-forwarding it would have moved the root checkout's HEAD under a parallel session, which is the shared-checkout hazard the same PR documents. The `.gitignore` protection becomes active in the root as soon as someone syncs.

add.issue.name: agent-coord: retire the file-claim system — the worktree is the boundary now

edit.description.md:
The claim system (`claim` / `release` / `status` / `check-clean` in `tools/agent-coord.py`, state in the gitignored `.agents/claims.json`) existed to stop two agents editing one file in a shared checkout. A worktree per ticket makes the filesystem the boundary instead, so claims are now a second mechanism that is wrong exactly where it matters.

Measured 2026-10-01, across the eight open branches — all built in one root checkout between 19:03 and 19:45:

- `.agents/claims.json` read `{}` the whole time. No agent held any claim while the collisions below happened.
- Neither worktree has a `.agents/` directory at all, because it is gitignored. A new worktree cannot read or write claims.
- `check-clean` run from inside `.work/3EEXMRK-bbprs-review-state` returns `clean` for the file that agent was editing. `nearest_git` (`tools/agent-coord.py:791`) requires `os.path.isdir('.git')`, and a worktree's `.git` is a file, so it walks up to the root checkout and reports *its* status.

**Remove:** `claim`, `release`, `release-all`, `status`, `check-clean`, and the `check-clean` step in `AGENTS.md`'s "Working tree" section.

**Keep:** `id`, `note`, `instance-note`, `workspace`, `dispatch`, `role-*`, `personal`, `ctx`, `news`, and the lock file, which still serialises the writers that remain.

## The part worktrees do not replace

Decide this before deleting anything, or the guard is lost rather than replaced. Two agents editing the same tracked file in *different* worktrees do not collide in the checkout — they collide at merge. Live from 2026-10-01, all open, all needing hand-resolution at merge time:

| file | tickets | size |
|------|---------|------|
| `personal/Xonok/STATUS.md` | `3EEXMRK`, `58MXTGY`, `FZDMC84` | 1 conflicting hunk (3EEXMRK × 58MXTGY) |
| `tools/taskview/SPEC.md` | `EY72YA9`, `X06YVNP` | 2 hunks, both authors already cross-reference each other |
| `AGENTS.md` | `58MXTGY`, `FZDMC84` | merges clean today |

Proposed replacement for the per-file claim on shared state files: `personal/<person>/{STATUS,HISTORY,TASKS}.md` are written by the secretary **at merge time**, not carried on feature branches. That takes STATUS.md out of every branch's diff, which is where all three of tonight's conflicts came from. Needs the human's ruling — it changes what a Done ticket is allowed to contain.

Do not close `8FVW49J` as part of this. It is the prerequisite: until it lands, `check-clean` cannot be trusted even in the root checkout.

Verification 2026-10-02: the drain the human ran is **half done**, and one finding changes how this ticket's blast radius should be read.

## What drained, and what did not

Run the detector from this ticket's own branch against the live board:

| Actor | Stranded | State |
|---|---|---|
| `opencode/mechanic` | 8 | **Drained** — committed today 07:54 (`CMGDFZF`, `VTJVHMY` creations included) |
| `space-bunny-free/mechanic` | 1 | **Drained** — committed today 07:45 |
| `opencode/paul` | **31** | **Still stranded**, last written 2026-09-29 |
| `paul` | **1** | **Still stranded**, written 07:43 today |

So 9 of 41 events landed; **32 are still stranded**, and the larger half — everything `opencode/paul` wrote on 2026-09-29 — did not. A third actor named plain `paul` registered itself at 07:43 and stopped without syncing, so an attempt on the paul half was started and abandoned rather than never made.

The 8 mechanic events include the `CMGDFZF` and `VTJVHMY` creations this ticket named as load-bearing, so **2 of the 3 orphans are resolved.** `QN1N82Y`'s creation is still stranded, and it is the one this ticket's own description singles out as reachable only from the pending file.

## The finding that matters more than the count

**The stranded state is invisible on the machine that has it.** `epiq_issue_list` and `epiq_issue_get` return `QN1N82Y` in Todo, and return `GBNEWPS` as `isClosed: true` carrying a `Solution:` comment — all of it sourced from the on-disk pending file, none of it from any committed log. Checked directly against `__epiq_state__`: `QN1N82Y` appears in **no** committed event log at all, and neither does `GBNEWPS`'s close or paul's `Solution:` comment (the committed record holds only its creation and two secretary comments).

So this ticket frames the blast radius as *missing `add.issue` events*, which is true and is the smaller half. The worse half is invisible in both directions and is the inverse failure:

- a fresh clone has **no `QN1N82Y`** — a filed, tagged, human-input-needed ticket that simply does not exist;
- a fresh clone has **`GBNEWPS` open in Todo with no `Solution:` comment** — an implemented, spec-backed xlint rule reading as work never started.

**This is why nobody noticed for three days, and it is a gap in this ticket's own detector.** `tools/epiq-pending.py` compares pending against committed, so it correctly says "created only here" — but it has no notion of *the local read path also serving uncommitted events*, so nothing it reports distinguishes "this machine can see it" from "this is durable". A second report against a **fresh clone** of the state branch would show the actual damage, and that is where `GBNEWPS` and `QN1N82Y` diverge from the count.

add.issue.comment.md:
Third data point on the `skipped: true` symptom, and it does **not** reproduce it — 2026-10-03, `opencode/secretary`.

## What happened this session

| call | what preceded it | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `actor_assume`, then `issue_comment_add`, then `issue_close` | `createdCommit: true`, `pushed: true`, `d5ee23d` |
| 2 | immediately after, no new write | `createdCommit: false`, `pushed: false`, **no `skipped` field** |

Both of that session's writes are in the committed log — verified by reading the events file, not by trusting the return value: `add.issue.comment` `01M40QBY…` and `close.issue` `01M3YV0CAM6ZEKB0VSC5DZ8NB1` are its last two lines, and all 4 lines of the leftover pending file are already present in it.

So: a single sync flushed two writes, and the extra drain had nothing to do and said so. Taken with the table in the previous comment, a sync called *immediately after a write* skipped 2 times out of 3 and did not skip the third.

## The reading I would change the diagnosis to

**It looks like a race, not a one-call lag.** A lag would skip deterministically on the call after a write; this skipped twice and not once, on the same sequence of steps. A pending file written by the MCP tool while `epiq_sync` is already reading is the shape that fits: the sync sees nothing new, reports success, and the next call finds the event sitting in the file it never read. It should therefore be intermittent, and worse under load — three `opencode/secretary` sessions were live this morning, all writing the same actor's log.

The practical advice is unchanged and is the part worth mechanising: **`skipped: true` is a signal to retry, not a verdict that there was nothing to do**, because it returns `status: success` and a session that walks away on it loses its last write silently. `createdCommit: false` with no `skipped` is the honest no-op and needs no retry. A drain script should loop until it sees `createdCommit: true` *or* a no-op, not sync once and continue.

## One thing the detector half should know

A drained pending file is **left on disk**, not deleted. `2cs40bjsw0d5m0a2zrw6bcdqm5~pending-…jsonl` (Sep 29) still sits beside its committed `2cs40bjsw0d5m0a2zrw6bcdqm5.jsonl` (Oct 2), byte-identical to what was committed, and my own pending file is in the same state right now. So *a pending file existing* is not a stranded signal — only its content being absent from the committed log is. Anything reporting "N stranded" off file presence will report a growing false count every time anyone drains successfully.

add.issue.name: A dev-version bypass, so a library under development can be tested against a live project

edit.description.md:
XLib has no sanctioned way for a running project to consume a library from `dev/`. Two rules combine to make it impossible by construction:

- `AGENTS.md:91` — libraries never use unversioned imports, and the only exception is a test *inside* the dev folder itself.
- `doc/library-structure.md:41-43` — dev folders are not packages; they are reached "by path, not by being a package".

So `dev/<library>/` is reachable from its own tests and from nothing else. All five dev libraries (`xconf`, `xcsv`, `xprod`, `xschema`, `xtest`) develop this way and **none has ever been exercised against a running application**.

## Why it matters

The workflow this repo exists for is: develop a library → test it where it runs → release it. XLib currently supports only the last step, so the middle one has no mechanism at all. A library can only be validated by a synthetic test, never by the application that will actually use it — which is the opposite of how the human works.

It is also blocked behind `1ZY2Q5Q`: `release.py` resolves dev folders at the wrong path, so **nothing has been releasable since 2026-09-17** (`xlib/` holds six releases, all predating the move). Until that is fixed, a bypass is not a convenience — it is the only path from a `dev/` library to a running project at all.

## What the human proposed

Symlinks inside XLib, so there is a folder holding dev-version entry points and a project can import a library from it directly, with no release in between. Still open: the folder's name and location, whether it is tracked or generated, and how `xlib/__init__.py` resolution should treat it.

## Alternatives worth choosing between

| Option | Shape | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Dev symlink folder | a folder of symlinks into `dev/`; projects import from it | cheapest to build; a symlink is a tracked file carrying a path, which the repo's own path rule (`7HP67R2`) discourages |
| Pin file | extend the existing `xlib_pins` hook — `_resolve()` already looks for one, but it maps a name to a *version*, not to a dev folder | no new paths in the tree; touches the resolution path every import goes through |
| Documented `sys.path` entry | no XLib code change; the project's launcher prepends `dev/`, and `AGENTS.md:91`'s exception clause is widened to cover it | smallest change, but every consumer repeats the incantation and the import line differs between dev and released |

Whichever is chosen, the **rule change is half the work**: a mechanism with no amendment to `AGENTS.md:91` leaves the library's own AGENTS.md forbidding the thing being built.

## Concretely waiting on this

`xhttp` — an HTTP library being hand-written now in `Space-Traveller/lib/`, destined for `XLib/dev/xhttp/` once it is decent, with Traveller as the live test case. That move is blocked on this ticket: without it, `xhttp` can be released-and-pinned but never developed-against.

Two things worth keeping cheap for that move, noted here so they are not rediscovered later:

- **Write it single-file.** The bundler prefixes internal module names (`csv_tok_tokenize`), so a one-file library is completely unaffected. The constraint only bites once it is split into `_/` internals, and then the public API must be *defined* in the entry file rather than re-exported.
- **Keep reach-ins low.** What makes the move expensive is not the import line in `server.py` (one line) but every place that reaches *into* the library's request state — `server.py`, `server/Chat/api.py` and `lib/websocket.py` all do. Fewer of those is the honest measure of how well the "no bundled state" goal went, and it is what keeps the eventual move to XLib cheap.

## Related

- `1ZY2Q5Q` — `release.py` resolves dev folders at the wrong path; every release fails. The amplifier here.
- `Z491RDN` — the patches-file design, which needed to know how a release lands in git.

add.issue.name: epiq-pending: a stranded close or comment exits 0 "clean" and names no ticket — only missing creations are reported

edit.description.md:
The detector half of `FZDMC84` landed in `9a74e5b` (merged 2026-10-08). It reports **missing creations**. It does not report **missing state transitions**, which is the half that made the failure invisible for three days — and `FZDMC84`'s own thread names this as the part it closed without building.

## Reproduced, not inferred

Fixture: a ticket whose `add.issue` **is committed**, whose `close.issue` and `Solution:` comment are **only in a pending file**, pending file backdated to 10s.

```
$ python3 tools/epiq-pending.py
exit: 0
  epiq project 01PROJ: no stranded events (2 events in flight, not yet synced)
clean
```

Exit **0**, the word **clean**, while the ticket's close and its comment exist in no committed log on any machine. Backdate the same fixture to 2h and the tool does notice — it prints `2/2 events  actor bbbb…  last written 2h ago / add.issue.comment, close.issue` — but **still names no ticket**, where the creation-loss half prints `created only here: ISSUE1  xlint frontmatter rule`.

## The asymmetry is the bug

`_pending_report` (`tools/epiq-pending.py:106`) builds `row["created"]` by filtering `_kind(e) == "add.issue"` (`:122`), and `_print_rows` (`:139`) is the only thing that turns an id into a human-readable subject. So:

| loss | reported | ticket named? |
|------|----------|---------------|
| creation stranded | orphan section, `created only here:` | yes |
| close / comment / move stranded | stranded count + kinds | **no** |

`CREATING_KINDS` vs `REFERENCING_KINDS` (`:6-8`) already draw the line: `close.issue`, `add.issue.comment`, `move.node`, `edit.title`, `edit.description`, `add.issue.tag` are all referencing kinds, so an event of any of them can be stranded while its target's creation is perfectly committed — and the tool has no vocabulary for that at all.

## Why the second row is the dangerous one

This is `GBNEWPS`, quoted from `FZDMC84`'s thread: `epiq_issue_get` returned it **closed with a `Solution:` comment** and `QN1N82Y` as a **filed ticket in Todo** — both sourced from the on-disk pending file, neither in any committed log. A fresh clone therefore had **no `QN1N82Y` at all**, and had `GBNEWPS` **open in Todo with no `Solution:` comment**: an implemented, spec-backed xlint rule reading as work never started. Neither reads as an orphan. Both read as *fine*, from the only machine that has the data.

The stranded-count split is deliberate and I am not asking to remove it — `FZDMC84` records why: a check that fires on the calling agent's own unsynced writes every session is a check that gets ignored. The problem is that the carve-out's subject is a **count**, and a count without a subject cannot be triaged. An agent reading `2 events in flight` has no way to learn that one of them is the close of a ticket it believes is shipped.

## What would falsify this

If a clone of the state branch can be shown to *preserve* pending events — i.e. durability does not in fact depend on the commit — then the whole framing is wrong and the tool is correct to ignore mutations. Nothing I know contradicts that, but I have not tested it, and it is the premise the ticket rests on.

## Scope

- Name the affected issue for stranded `REFERENCING_KINDS` events, not only `add.issue` — reuse `_issue_titles`, which already reads pending files (`tools/epiq-pending.py:58`) so a subject resolves even when the creation is stranded too.
- A second report that names the **divergence**, not the loss: for each stranded referencing event, what a clone sees versus what this machine sees. That is the report `FZDMC84` promised and did not deliver.
- Keep the age-based in-flight/st-stranded split as it is. Tests in `tools/test/`, per `doc/development.md`.

## Related

- `FZDMC84` — closed 2026-10-08; this is its undelivered half, recorded on the ticket before closing.
- `AZHG0FK` — the accepted-risk ruling this supersedes.
- `AK633QC` — a linter reporting 0 over content it should have flagged; same shape, different tool.

add.issue.name: Add xlib_dev override: run real code against an unreleased library

edit.description.md:
`from xlib_dev import xcsv` resolves a bare name to `dev/xcsv/xcsv.py` instead of the newest file in `xlib/`, so one import line is the only change between testing a prerelease and testing what users get.

Resolved through `__getattr__` rather than a file per library: adding a library needs no change, and the caller gets the real module object rather than a copy of its names taken at import time. The library keeps its own module name, so `dev/xcsv/xcsv.py:31`'s `from ._ import csv_tok,csv_ser` still resolves.

**Covers the caller's import only.** A library's own imports of other libraries stay pinned to released versions, which the libraries-are-pinned rule requires — testing a dev xcsv still gets a released xschema. A dev library depending on another dev library is fine and intended; only the dev to release boundary is policed, and by release.py refusing to package the library.

**Not a release.** The dev surface is a superset: internals appear as themselves (`xcsv.csv_tok`) where the bundle renames them (`xcsv.csv_tok_tokenize`). Passing through `xlib_dev` is not proof of passing against the release that follows.

Enforcement is separate: xlint repo-specific rules, the `xlib_dev` rule itself, and release.py refusing a dev dependency are filed as their own tickets.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `xlib_dev/__init__.py` resolves any name backed by a `dev/<name>/<name>.py` through a module-level `__getattr__`, aliasing the real module into `sys.modules` so relative imports inside the library still resolve. Chosen over a file per library: adding a library then needs no change, and the caller gets the module object rather than a name snapshot. Verified from a project outside the repo that swapping one import line moves the load between `dev/xcsv/xcsv.py` and `xlib/xcsv_1_1_0.py`. 12 tests in `xlib_dev/tests/`, mutation-checked — breaking the import target fails 4 of them. Committed `b0214a4` on master, epiq ref `ASTXNPG`.

Two limits worth keeping in view, both documented in `doc/library-structure.md`:

- It covers the caller's import only. A library's own imports of other libraries stay pinned to released versions, so a dev xcsv under test still gets a released xschema. Dev-to-dev is fine and intended; only the dev-to-release boundary is policed, and that belongs to release.py.
- It is not a release. The dev surface is a superset — `xcsv.csv_tok` where the bundle emits `xcsv.csv_tok_tokenize` — so passing through `xlib_dev` is not proof of passing against the release that follows.

One test here already enforces part of what the enforcement tickets cover: `test_no_released_file_references_the_override` scans `xlib/*.py` for the string. When the lint rule lands it should move there rather than be duplicated.

add.issue.name: xlint --watch never reloads .xlintignore — a newly un-ignored file stays invisible and a newly ignored one keeps being reported

edit.description.md:
## The gap

`--watch` reads `.xlintignore` once, at startup, and never again. `main()` builds the
`_Exclusions` object once (`tools/xlint/xlint.py:1142`) and hands the same frozen instance
to both watchers (`make_watcher`, `:1076`), which hold it as `self.exclusions` for the
life of the process. Editing the ignore file mid-session changes nothing until restart.

Proved both directions on a scratch tree, 2026-10-12:

**Newly un-ignored content is never picked up.** Start with `sub/` excluded, run
`xlint . --watch`, then empty `.xlintignore`:

```
=== xlint ===
clean
=== xlint ===
ok.py:2: indented with spaces          <- only ok.py reacts
1 problem(s)
```

`sub/bad.py` stays invisible, although a fresh process on the same tree reports both:

```
ok.py:2: indented with spaces
sub/bad.py:2: indented with spaces
2 problem(s)
```

**Newly ignored content keeps being reported.** Start un-ignored, add `sub/` while
watching, then touch `sub/bad.py` — the line keeps appearing, because the stale
exclusion set still says the file is linted.

## Why it is more than a restart

Restarting is the workaround, and it costs the thing watch mode exists for: the
inotify watch set is built once in `__init__` from the same stale exclusions
(`watch_tree`, `:999-1006`). A directory excluded at startup was never registered,
so **its inotify watch does not exist even if the rules were reloaded** — the fix has
to rebuild the watch set, not just re-read the file. The `_PollWatcher` fallback does
re-walk per poll (`:1065`), so reloading rules would mostly be enough there, but the
two backends then need to agree.

## Shape of the fix

- Reload `_Exclusions` when a `.xlintignore` changes — mtime-stamp the exclusion roots
  the same way `_PollWatcher` stamps files, so one mechanism serves both backends.
- Rebuild the inotify watch set on reload; dropping watches for newly excluded
  directories matters as much as adding them for newly included ones (the reverse
  direction leaks inotify watches and keeps re-linting dead subtrees).
- A `.xlintignore` can appear or vanish, not just change — `find_exclusion_roots`
  (`:131`) walks upward, so a file added *above* the lint root also governs the run.
- Decide whether a reload is silent or prints a line. Silent is consistent with the
  rest of the UI, which redraws only on change.

## Worth noting alongside

`main()` builds exclusions from `args.paths[0]` alone (`:1142`) and passes them to
`lint_files` for every path, so a single invocation spanning two repos is governed
only by the first one's chain. Related, and cheap to fix in the same place.

Refs the `.xlintignore` mechanism from `AK633QC` / `Q93KNA9`.

add.issue.name: xhttp websocket lifecycle: idle connections die at 60s, handler exceptions kill the socket, on_open errors write HTTP into the upgraded stream

edit.description.md:
Three faults in `dev/xhttp`, all found while integrating xhttp into Traveller and all reproducible against xhttp on its own. None is consumer-side.

## 1. An idle websocket is killed at exactly 60s

`dev/xhttp/_/server.py:32` applies `s.settimeout(60)` to every **accepted** socket, websocket upgrades included. `websocket.receiver` sits in `client.recv()`, so an otherwise healthy connection raises `TimeoutError`, and the blanket `except Exception` treats it as fatal and tears the connection down.

Measured on a bare xhttp server with a client that sends nothing after the handshake: **EOF at t=+60.1s**, with `on_close` called. Server-to-client traffic does not help - the receiver is waiting on the other direction.

This is a regression against the HTTP implementation Traveller is replacing: `dumb_http` puts its timeout on the *listening* socket only (`lib/dumb_http.py:217`), accepted sockets get none, and frames are read from a buffered file object that never times out.

Suggested fix: keep the timeout for the request/keep-alive phase, then clear it (`settimeout(None)`) once the connection has been upgraded.

## 2. Any exception from the caller's `on_message` is treated as a fatal transport error

`dev/xhttp/_/websocket.py:75-94` wraps `_recv` and `on_message` in one `except Exception` that calls `on_close` and shuts the sender down. Verified: an `on_message` that raises a plain `RuntimeError` closes the socket (client sees EOF).

A genuine transport error (`TimeoutError`, `ConnectionResetError`, `HTTPBodyIncomplete`) should end the connection. An exception from the consumer's own handler should be reported and the receive loop should continue - today a one-line application bug takes down every open connection.

## 3. If `on_open` raises, xhttp writes an HTTP 500 into an already-upgraded websocket stream

`dev/xhttp/_/server.py:108` calls `on_open` *after* the 101 handshake has been sent. An exception propagates to `wrap_handler`, whose generic handler does `response.send_response(client,500)`.

Captured on the client, immediately after the handshake headers:

```
b'HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error\r\ndate: ...\r\ncontent-length: 0\r\n\r\n'
```

That is a second HTTP response inside a websocket stream. Any conforming client sees a protocol error, which is very hard to diagnose from the browser side.

Suggested fix: once the 101 has gone out, a failure can only be reported by closing the socket - `wrap_handler` must not try to send an HTTP response on an upgraded connection.

## Smaller, same area

- `receiver` treats a close frame (`op 8`) as `break` and never calls `on_close`. A consumer that relies on `on_close` to release per-connection state silently leaks it on every clean disconnect.
- The accept loop (`_/server.py:27-38`) no longer has a timeout on the listening socket, so `sock.accept()` cannot be interrupted. `dumb_http` set 1s for exactly that reason.

## Why it matters beyond Traveller

Traveller's symptom was a websocket that drops immediately and reconnects on a timer, which is what sent this investigation. Items 1 and 2 each turn an application bug or a quiet connection into a total disconnect, and item 3 corrupts the stream in a way that hides the real cause.

add.issue.name: tools/pybundle/bundler_impl.py has a committed syntax error — the bundler cannot be imported, so no library can be released

edit.description.md:
`tools/pybundle/bundler_impl.py` does not parse. It is committed that way on
master, so **nothing can be released** — `release.py` bundles through it.

```
$ python3 -c "import py_compile; py_compile.compile('tools/pybundle/bundler_impl.py', doraise=True)"
py_compile.PyCompileError: Sorry: IndentationError: unindent does not match
any outer indentation level (bundler_impl.py, line 225)
```

`bundler.py` has a relative-import fallback for direct invocation, so both
entry points hit it:

```
$ python3 tools/pybundle/bundler.py --help
ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package
...
IndentationError: unindent does not match any outer indentation level
```

## The defect

Around line 223, one `continue` carries an extra tab:

```
223: <TAB><TAB>ast.GeneratorExp)):        continuation of the if condition
224: <TAB><TAB><TAB><TAB>continue        <- one tab too many
225: <TAB><TAB><TAB>if isinstance(...)   <- dedent to a level never opened
226: <TAB><TAB><TAB><TAB>for t in c.targets:
```

Line 224 belongs at 3 tabs to match its `if`.

## Where it came from

Introduced by `dc3d4fd` (`5ZZRJ23`, *"formatting pass: fix all xlint
violations across repo"*). Verified: `git show dc3d4fd^:tools/pybundle/bundler_impl.py`
parses cleanly, and the current file matches `HEAD` with no uncommitted diff —
so this is what master has, not a working-tree accident.

Worth noting what that implies: an automated "fix all lint violations" pass
made a committed Python file unparseable, and the commit merged. A pass that
rewrites code should be checked by parsing every file it touches.

## It is detectable — the tests already fail

`tools/pybundle/test/test_bundler.py` dies at import for exactly this reason:

```
File "tools/pybundle/test/test_bundler.py", line 5, in <module>
    from pybundle import bundler
  ...
IndentationError: unindent does not match any outer indentation level
```

So the suite is not blind to this; it has evidently not been run since the
formatting pass. Two separate questions worth answering separately: fix the
tab, and decide what should have run the tests before that merge.

## Why it matters right now

Space-Traveller is on `from xlib_dev import xhttp` and cannot move to
`from xlib import xhttp` until xhttp is released — and xhttp cannot be
released until the bundler runs. This is the blocker on that swap.

Note the existing `1ZY2Q5B` (release.py resolves the dev folder at the wrong
path) is a different defect in the same journey and will need attention
separately once the bundler imports at all.

add.issue.name: xlint reports clean for any file in a worktree — same nearest_git defect as 8FVW49J, and it makes a style gate fail open

edit.description.md:
xlint reports **clean** for any file inside a git worktree, so a lint run there proves nothing. Found by being misled by it: a file with 36 xlint problems was linted inside a worktree, reported clean, and merged to `master` failing.

## Cause

The same one `8FVW49J` records for `agent-coord check-clean` — `nearest_git` does not treat a worktree root as a repository root, because a worktree's `.git` is a **file** rather than a directory. Anything gated on that lookup silently treats everything as excluded or ignored, and xlint's answer becomes `clean` with exit 0.

`8FVW49J`'s title scopes it to check-clean, so this is filed separately rather than folded in — different tool, different symptom, and the one that matters more here, because a false clean on a **style gate** looks like passing CI.

## The failure mode that hurts

Lint is the thing people trust to catch what they cannot see. A tab-versus-space indentation violation is invisible in a diff and invisible on screen, which is exactly why the linter exists. A linter that reports clean on 36 real violations is worse than no linter: it converts "I checked" into a false claim.

It also fails silently in the one direction that matters. Nothing errors, nothing warns, the exit code is 0.

## Worked example

`tools/pybundle/SPEC.md`, 2026-10-14:

- linted inside `.work/6MFX0Z1-pybundle-spec` — reported `clean`
- the same bytes linted in the root checkout — **36 problems**: list continuations indented with spaces, alignment inside tab-indented code blocks, no final newline

Merged as `24e1856` in that state and fixed in `d9528b0`.

## What a fix needs to cover

Live documentation describes a repo layout that stopped existing on 2026-09-17, when `xconf/`, `xcsv/`, `xschema/`, `xtest/` and `xprod/` moved under `dev/` (`da1d163`). The canonical references — `doc/library-structure.md` and `readme.md` — are correct; these are not.

- **`doc/plans/xaudit.md`** — the classification rule read *"Library: top-level `<name>/<name>.py` (e.g. `xcsv/xcsv.py`)"*. This one matters more than a stale example: it is the rule that decides which paths get library checks, so implementing xAudit from it as written would have excluded every library in the repo. Its checks table carried `<lib>/__init__.py`, `<lib>/VERSIONS.md` and `<lib>/<lib>.py` with the same omission.
- **`doc/plans/xaudit.md`** — *"Decided: `pybundle/` stays at root."* It did not stay at root. The same 2026-09-17 moves that created `dev/` also put `xlint/`, `release/` **and** `pybundle/` under `tools/`, so by the rule three lines above, all three are tools today.
- **`doc/reviews/README.md`** — *"The bundler that exists is the five-phase implementation in `tools/pybundle/bundler.py` + `bundler_impl.py`, described by `tools/pybundle/SPEC.md`, with 7 fixtures that pass."* Deleted 2026-10-14 (`5e87ae8`). This is the index a reader is pointed at before reading any review, and it was pointing them at a file that does not exist.

`doc/reviews/pybundle-*.md`, `doc/reviews/xcsv-81f355dd.md` and `doc/audits/2026-09-11-workspace.md` also name `xcsv/xcsv.py` and friends. Nothing lints prose for stale paths, and the `dev/` move landed as two commits four minutes apart on 2026-09-17 — `8a67eeb` handled the tool side, `da1d163` the library side, and the docs were only half-updated. That is the same pair of commits that broke `release.py`, tracked as `1ZY2Q5Q`; this ticket is the documentation half of that move.

add.issue.comment.md:
**One more decision, and it corrects a statement the spec got wrong rather than adding a capability (`d412f9a`).**

The spec's *Edge cases* entry said name collisions "between globals of different files" are assumed not to happen and are neither detected nor fixed. That named the wrong surface. Every global a file **defines** is prefixed with that file's prefix, and prefixes are unique because R1.6 processes each file once — so two defined globals cannot collide. The entry protected a class that is empty by construction.

The names that are **not** prefixed are the ones a file binds through a non-local import, and every one of them lands in the same namespace once the bundle is one file. Two files sharing nothing but a habit of naming things `math` now meet, and whichever is inlined second wins. The root is the sharpest case, because its prefix is empty: the root doing `from local_func import math` writes `math = local_func__math` over the top-level `math` another file bound with `import math`.

**The ruling: none of it is fixed, detected, or reported.** A warning was considered and declined — the bundler does see every import statement it inlines, so collecting unprefixed bound names and reporting a duplicate is cheap, but the tool's position is that it is opinionated about what it bundles, not about what it can prove about the result. The human's words were that a warning is optional and by no means necessary.

It is written down as **D19** so that a broken bundle has somewhere to point, and so a later session does not read the silence as an oversight and go build the collision detection this rewrite deliberately does without.

One asymmetry is named rather than smoothed over: D9 aliases a non-local **name** import to the importing file's prefixed global, so it cannot collide, while a non-local **module** import is not aliased — prefixing it means rewriting every use of the name in the file, not only attribute accesses, which is a larger change than the collision it prevents.

No test change: the review already recorded name collisions as deliberately untested, and D19 is the requirement that says so.

add.issue.name: pybundle: mixed tab/space indentation — the block-closing rule reads it as "indents less", so scope tracking silently ends the block

edit.description.md:
Human, 2026-10-15: "the bundler might break if files have mixed indentation
types. It might be reasonable to give a warning in that case, but still attempt
to bundle."

Not hypothetical. Three facts, all reproduced locally on 2026-10-15:

1. **Python accepts the file.** A module with `def f():` tab-indented and
	`def g():` space-indented parses (`ast.parse`) and runs. The check is per
	indentation token against the stack top, not per file.
2. **`tokenize` handles it correctly.** `INDENT '\t'`, `INDENT '\t\t'`,
	`DEDENT`, `DEDENT`, then `INDENT '    '`, `INDENT '       '`, `DEDENT`,
	`DEDENT` — the block structure is right. So D1/D2's stated source of truth
	does not lose information here.
3. **The comparison D2 specifies does not survive it.** D2: "The block runs
	until a statement indents less than the opener." The `indent` field is a
	*string* (D16 shape; the review chose string over column count precisely so
	D2 could use INDENT/DEDENT). In Python `'\t' < '    '` is **True** — tab is
	0x09, space is 0x20. So a tab-indented body under a space-indented opener
	reads as *less than* the opener and the block closes on its first line.

Consequence if implemented as written: everything inside that function is
recorded as module-level scope, so R4's scope rule translates names that should
be local. **No error, no diagnostic — a bundle that is wrong.** That is the
worst failure class this tool has.

## Second, separate exposure: inlined indentation

An import inside a function is inlined at the *importing* file's indentation
(D8/`test_indented_local_import_is_inlined_even_under_a_false_condition`), so the
inlined body has to be re-indented from the module's own convention into the
caller's. The spec does not say who performs that conversion, or what happens
when the two conventions differ.

## Three ways to rule it — the human's is one of them

- **A. Warn on stderr, still bundle** (the human's proposal). Consistent with
	the accepted limit already in D9, where a non-local star import "will
	sometimes produce a bundle that does not work, and says so on stderr rather
	than refusing".
- **B. Make D2 match INDENT/DEDENT instead of comparing strings.** Then mixing
	costs nothing at all — it is already what the tokenizer emits — and the
	warning is purely informational for the reader. `pybundle-tests-pass1-2.md`
	says the `indent` field was chosen as a string so D2's comparison *could*
	use INDENT/DEDENT tokens "without either form having to be re-derived". B
	makes that the rule rather than the reason.
- **C. Refuse.** Costs every file that mixes conventions across blocks, and
	Python runs those fine.

B is not in tension with A — they compose. What A alone does not do is stop the
scope-tracking failure, only announce it.

## Two spec edits either way

- **D14 says "Three of them exist"** and enumerates them. A warning is the
	fourth, and the sentence has to change.
- **D19 records a warning as *declined*** for name collisions, with the human's
	own reasoning ("considered a warning optional and not necessary"). That is a
	different failure class — collisions are a property of the result, mixed
	indentation is a property of the input — so this is not a reversal. But two
	adjacent decisions about warnings reading opposite ways needs one sentence
	each saying which is which, or the next reader will read a contradiction.

## What is inference, not verified

That an implementer would reach for the string comparison is inferred from D2's
wording and D16's shape; the implementer does not exist yet. Fact 2 is the
counter-evidence: reading D2 as token-matching makes all of this a non-issue.

add.issue.name: pybundle: D9 and D19 still describe the rebinding mechanism the F13 ruling removed — four places, an implementer will build them

edit.description.md:
From `doc/reviews/pybundle-tests-pass1-2.md`, F23. **This is a repair list, not a
question — the human has already answered it.** The F13 ruling removed the
rebinding mechanism; D9 and D19 still describe it in four places, and an
implementer reading `SPEC.md` top to bottom today will build the rebindings.
Nothing blocks on a decision here.

## The four places

1. **D9, the local bullet** — "the importing file gains a rebinding:
	`count = helper__count`". There is no rebinding. Under F13 the file's block
	gets no added statement at all.
2. **D9, the non-local bullet** — "the statement stays, with the bound name
	aliased: `from pathlib import join as A__join`". It does not stay; it becomes
	`import pathlib`, because `join` is now reached as `pathlib.join`.
3. **D9, the second paragraph** — "A name imported into a file becomes that
	file's global, so R3's prefix applies to it." It does not become a global.
	It is a use, and the prefixed name is the one the value came from.
4. **D9's divergence note + D19's fourth bullet** — the root-level rebinding
	collision (`from local_func import math` writing `math = local_func__math`).
	No such statement is emitted, so the collision cannot happen, and with it
	goes the only collision D19 gives where the root's empty prefix is the cause.

## What survives, and is now the only statement of the rule

D19's *exception* paragraph. The mechanism is unchanged; only the conclusion
moves, because there is nothing to prefix:

> A non-local **name** import is aliased to the importing file's prefixed
> global — `from pathlib import join as A__join`

becomes `pathlib.join`. That is what
`test_a_name_import_from_a_non_local_module_binds_an_unprefixed_name` pins.

## Cost if skipped

Six of the 138 tests were deleted or rewritten because they asserted the
rebinding. An implementer who follows the spec instead of the tests rebuilds it,
and the tests then fail for a reason that is not a bug — the same trap F16's
missing field names set, recorded in the review as "an implementer is free to
choose otherwise and two tests will fail for a reason that is not a bug".

Same append-only discipline as the pass-1 append (`03c0e75`): write the repair
as a further decision section, leave the text above untouched.

add.issue.name: pybundle: three name-import shapes have no stated answer — local star import, a name the module does not define, a name imported at function scope

edit.description.md:
From `doc/reviews/pybundle-tests-pass1-2.md`, F22 and F24. **Three shapes the
spec does not answer, all of which produce a silently broken bundle rather than
an error.** F22 leaves one test unwritten; F24 leaves two. None blocks the suite
as it stands.

## F22 — a star import of a local module has no mechanism left

D9 gave `from helper import *` its rebindings: "emits one rebinding per global
of `helper`". F13 removed rebindings for `from x import y`, and a star import
cannot use the replacement either — **it names nothing, so there is no use to
rewrite into `helper__x`.**

The review's proposal: put every defined global of the inlined module into the
importing file's rename table, so each use of `count` is rewritten to
`helper__count` as it is read. Same bundle D9's rebindings produced, no
statement emitted, consistent with F13 rather than against it. The review
declined to pick between the two, because they differ on whether a file that
*also* defines `count` gets a conflict.

**The ruling needed:** rebindings, or rename table — and if rename table, what
happens when the importing file defines the same name itself.

## F24-A — a name the module does not define

`from helper import thing`, where `thing` is something `helper` itself imported.
The bundler checks whether the target is a file; it is not; so it takes the name
branch and rewrites every use of `thing` to `helper__thing`. Nothing defines
that — `thing` is a non-local module name, and D19 leaves those unprefixed.

D9 already states this exact limit for star imports ("rebinding are emitted for
the inlined module's defined globals only"). The name-import case needs the same
sentence, or a ruling that it behaves differently.

## F24-B — a name imported at function scope

`from helper import count` inside a function. D9 is phrased about what a name
imported *into a file* is reached through, and is silent on whether function
scope changes it. Both readings happen to work: if scope does change it, the
name is in the enclosing scope's rename table and the uses resolve; if it does
not, the use is still rewritten to `helper__count` and resolves anyway.

The review's note is the right frame — "both readings happen to work, which is
why this one is cheap to answer and expensive to leave." Cheap now, before the
implementation hard-codes one.

## Also touched here

F19 — a function-local name import as a *binding form* in D2. Same question as
F24-B, from the scope-tracking side: D2 lists function-local `import` among the
forms that block translation, and nothing says whether a name import at
function scope joins that list. `test_a_function_local_name_import_blocks_the_rename`
is the missing test.

add.issue.name: pybundle: five spec edits the test pass already answered and nobody has written in — D16 field names, D13 argv, D1 clause, F18, the counting correction

edit.description.md:
From `doc/reviews/pybundle-tests-pass1-2.md`. **These need writing into
`SPEC.md`, not a decision** — the human has already answered each one, and the
review carries the answer. Listed separately from the ruling-needed tickets
because the work is mechanical and should not wait on a discussion.

## D16 — the two field names, proposed and not yet in the spec

F16 was answered: `statements` returns dictionaries, propose the field names.
These are the proposal. Until they are written in, **an implementer is free to
choose otherwise and two tests will fail for a reason that is not a bug.**

| Field | Holds | Why this spelling |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | the statement's source text, first line's indentation included, no trailing newline | D16 says "its text" — the spec's own word |
| `indent` | that same leading whitespace, **as a string** | D16 says "its indentation". A string, not a column count, because it round-trips exactly and there is no unit to agree on |

Two choices inside that, both the review's and both defensible: a multi-line
statement's `text` carries **every** line (R7 requires the text to survive
unchanged, and joining statements has to put the file back); `indent` is the
**first** physical line's whitespace, which D1 already states.

The alternative for `indent` is a column count, in which case a tab is eight
columns — that is what the tokenizer computes. **This is not a free choice:**
the string form is what makes `'\t' < '    '` a problem, and it is the hinge
the mixed-indentation ticket turns on. String + INDENT/DEDENT matching is safe;
string + comparison is not.

Nothing is proposed for `imports`' entries — D8's "in source order" is already
pinned behaviourally, and the review declined to invent four field names for it.

## D13 — the `cli` signature clause

F14's answer was a question back: the program name does not matter to the person
running it, only to what `__main__` hands `cli`. The suite proceeds with
**arguments only** — `cli(sys.argv[1:])`, so `cli(["--in", p, "--out", "-"])`
— because that is what `argparse.parse_args` takes. One clause settles it. If
the implementation uses `argparse` the choice is made for it and the clause is
belt and braces; ruling the other way is one literal per test, 16 of the 18 CLI
tests.

## D1 — the empty-line and comment clause

F17: empty lines and comment-only lines pass through unchanged; the rules about
what a statement is exist so a multi-line statement is not broken apart, **not
so that anything is removed.** The ruling is recorded in the tests; one clause
stops an implementer reading D1 narrowly.

## F18 — `pass` after a removed indented import

Not answered. D8's "removed entirely" and the Edge cases' `pass` rule disagree
about the one-line compound body. `test_indented_local_import_leaves_a_pass_where_it_was`
deliberately uses the form both readings agree on, so this is free to leave — but
it should be closed rather than open.

## The counting correction

`pybundle-tests-pass1.md` carries a blocking count that does not reconcile, and
the spec's *Open, and deliberately so* section says so. Reconciled in pass 2:
**six** flaws blocked tests entirely (F4–F8, F12); three blocked direct tests
only, resolved by a stated workaround rather than a decision (F1–F3); three
needed none (F9–F11). The "nine" and the "seven" counted the same twelve
differently. Six is the number that describes what actually stopped the work, and
the spec's paragraph quoting the unreconciled count should be corrected rather
than left pointing at it.

add.issue.comment.md:
**RULED, human, 2026-10-15.** Verbatim: *"Using the tokenizer's INDENT/DEDENT is a reasonable way of interpreting my intent. Checking strings exactly is not necessary, or should come with the understanding that spaces and tabs need different handling."*

**This settles the mechanism question — option B from the description is the ruling.** D2 tracks blocks by matching the tokenizer's own INDENT/DEDENT tokens, not by comparing indentation strings. The scope-tracking failure described above cannot happen, and the `'\t' < '    '` hazard goes with it.

It also settles a choice recorded elsewhere. `EZAVYNM`'s D16 note says the `indent` field was chosen as a string rather than a column count *so that* D2 could use INDENT/DEDENT "without either form having to be re-derived" — that reasoning is now the decision rather than a rationale, and the two tickets should be read together.

## What the ruling does not reach: re-indentation on inline

Checked after the ruling, because it is the other place indentation crosses between files. An import inside a function is inlined at the *importing* file's indentation, so the inlined body carries the **callee's** convention into the **caller's** block. INDENT/DEDENT matching says nothing about that — it describes how a file's own blocks are read, not how one file's text is placed inside another.

**The finding: this one can produce a bundle that does not even parse.** Reproduced 2026-10-15:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| tabs-module inlined at module level of a space importer | runs |
| tabs-module inlined inside a 4-space function | runs |
| spaces-module inlined inside a tab function | runs |
| **tabs-module inlined at depth 8, sibling at column 16 written with spaces** | **`TabError: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation`** |
| tabs-module at depth 4, sibling at column 12 written with a tab | `TabError` |

The mechanism is exact: a tab at depth *n* is column `8n`, and after prefixing it sits at `8n + prefix`. A sibling written with spaces at that same column expresses the same depth two ways, and Python rejects it. **This is worse than the failure the ticket was filed about** — a wrong bundle is silent, an unparseable one fails immediately, but it fails in the *consumer's* import rather than at bundle time, which is a much longer way round to find out.

Two mitigating facts, both verified: a `TabError` is only reachable when **two lines in the same block share a depth and disagree on convention**, so the bundler cannot manufacture one out of files that each import cleanly on their own — the ambiguity has to arrive from the caller's own indentation meeting the callee's. And it needs the inline-at-depth path, which is the rarer shape.

## Open, and now narrow

1. **Does a warning survive the ruling?** On the scope question it is now noise — the blocks are tracked correctly, so there is nothing to report. On the inline question it is not: that is the case where output is genuinely at risk.
2. **If a warning stays, what condition fires it?** "A file mixes conventions" is the wrong trigger — it fires on files that bundle correctly (three of the five cases above) and can still miss the inlined depth collision, which depends on the *caller's* indentation, not the callee's. A trigger has to be about the inline step.
3. **What does the inline step do about the two conventions meeting?** Options that exist: re-indent the inlined body into the caller's convention; refuse that inline; let it through with a warning. The first is a real conversion the spec does not currently describe anywhere.

`EZAVYNM`'s D16 entry should note that `indent` is the **callee's** text as written, and that whatever re-indents it owns the conversion.

add.issue.comment.md:
**RULED, human, 2026-10-15 — the warning trigger.** Verbatim: *"I'd warn on tabs if indentation is inconsistent about space or tabs in general. If the root file uses tabs, so should all local ones it imports. From the perspective of warning the user, this is the simple approach, especially when combined with listing every file that differs from the root file's convention. (or the first file that has indentation). So essentially the warning should happen when ANY line contains any other indentation type than what the root file (or first file with indentation) has. This would trigger on spaces in a tab-indented project, but also on both used in the same line."*

## The rule, as stated

1. **Anchor**: whatever the **root file** uses, falling back to the **first file that has indentation** where the root has none.
2. **Trigger**: **any line** containing an indentation type other than the anchor's.
3. **Report**: list **every file** that differs from the anchor.
4. **Over-firing is intended** — the human says so. Spaces in a tab project trip it, and one line mixing both trips it.
5. **Warn, not refuse.** With the INDENT/DEDENT ruling above this is the tool's fourth diagnostic, so **D14's "Three of them exist" has to change**.

## The rule catches the inline case too — the root anchor is what does it

Not obvious from the trigger's wording. The depth-8 `TabError` from the previous comment has two *individually consistent* inputs: a tabs-module and a space-importer. Anchoring on the root means the callee disagrees with the root by construction, so **every tab-led line in it trips the warning**. The trigger catches the output hazard, not only mixed input — not by reasoning about inline, but by comparing against the root rather than each file's own habit.

The cost is the over-firing already accepted: a tabs-module inlined at depth 4 produces a bundle that **runs correctly** and still warns.

## What it cannot do

It is a warning, not a guard. The bundle is still written, so case J still ships a file that raises `TabError` in the consumer's import — now with a stderr line saying why. Whether that is the answer is what remains open: what the inline step does. Convert the callee's indentation into the caller's convention, refuse that inline, or let it through.

## Reachability of the "both in the same line" clause

Not theoretical, and reachable on **valid input**: `def f():` with body `'\t    return 1'` parses and runs, as does `'    \treturn 1'`. It fails only when a *sibling* at the same depth uses a different convention. So the clause catches real code rather than being defensive boilerplate.

add.issue.comment.md:
## One correction to "ANY line" — D1 already fixes it, free

A literal per-line scan fires on **bracket continuation lines**, whose leading whitespace Python ignores. Real example in this repo, `dev/xhttp/test/test_parity.py` lines 11, 12, 15, 17, 53, 54 — tab-then-spaces, continuations of one list literal spanning lines 1–33. The file parses and runs. A per-line scan warns on code that is fine.

**D1 is the fix and it is already written**: `tokenize` emits `NEWLINE` at a real statement end and `NL` inside brackets, and the spec builds statements on that distinction precisely so continuation lines are not misread. Scanning statements instead of lines costs nothing, keeps the warning meaning what the human means, and reuses a mechanism D1 already commits to.

## Cost on this repo: zero

Checked all **21 files under `dev/` that actually get inlined** — entry files plus `_/`, excluding `test/` and `compare/`. Mixed-leading-whitespace lines: **0**. Every inlined file is unanimously tab-led with no space-led line at all. **The rule fires on nothing here.** The only file in `dev/` that trips it is `test_parity.py`, which is not bundled.

So the implementation is cheap, the behaviour on XLib is silent, and the warning will matter when someone bundles a foreign library — which is the case a warning is for.

## Where this leaves the ticket

Both halves are now ruled: **INDENT/DEDENT** for block tracking, and **warn with the root-file anchor** for the trigger. Nothing further is needed here for the input-side rule.

The one question this leaves, which is taskview `#128` rather than this ticket: the warning is not a guard. Case J still ships a `TabError` bundle, now with a stderr line above it. The three options are unchanged — **convert** the callee's indentation into the caller's convention, **refuse** that inline, or **let it through**. The first is a conversion the spec describes nowhere, and it is the only one that fixes the output rather than describing it.

I'd say the root file is the most likely to match whatever the project conventions are, so taking it as the assumed default and calling out violations compared to that should be the most useful option that can be implemented cheaply. **RULED, human, 2026-10-15 — the warning's shape is now complete.** Two rulings, verbatim:

add.issue.comment.md:
**RULED, human, 2026-10-15 — alias. This reverses F13 and closes `F7KHKM8` outright.**

The chain: *"every import in python actually creates a name and I've been trying to avoid turning that into guaranteed bloat. Essentially, following python behaviour strictly would be the correct choice and would mean that every import involves a rebind."* → for non-local imports, *"there would have to be both an import and a bind... Separate statements are likely easier to maintain, since long import lines can be retained without splitting"* → then, on the collision evidence, **"Okay, let's go with the alias solution."**

## The mechanism

- **local** — import line deleted, one rebind per name: `server__ship__defs = server__defs`
- **non-local** — import line **rewritten with an alias**, no second statement: `from x import defs as A__defs`
- **star import of a local module** — the same rebind, one per defined global. A star import is *"just a more concise version of `from x import a,b,c...`"*, so it gets the same answer, not a special one.

The two-statement form was preferred first and then dropped because it does not remove the collision — it relocates it. `from x import defs` binds `defs` at top level whether or not anyone rebinds it, so the rebind copies whichever import won. Measured: two-statement gives `A__defs → FROM-Y`, `B__defs → FROM-Y`; alias gives `A__defs → FROM-X`, `B__defs → FROM-Y`. Alias also keeps long import lines on one line — `from x import a as A__a, b as A__b, c as A__c` — so the maintenance concern that motivated the two-statement form turns out not to apply here.

## All three questions answered by this, verified together

Built the bundle the ruling describes and ran it against real Python doing the same. **Three of three match.**

| Case | Bundle | Real Python |
|---|---|---|
| local star import, then shadowing (`count = 2`) | `2` | `2` |
| `from helper import Path`, `Path` being *helper's* own non-local import | resolves | resolves |
| `from helper import count` at function scope | `1`, correctly local | `1` |

1. **Star import + shadowing** works because the rebind is a **statement**, so a later `count = 2` overrides it in source order. That was the reading that failed under F13, and why F22 was unanswerable.
2. **F24-A is dissolved, not answered.** Under F13, a name the module does not define rewrote to `helper__Path`, which nothing defined. Now helper's own import is `from pathlib import Path as server__Path`, so `server__ship__Path = server__Path` has something to point at. D9's stated divergence for star imports survives unchanged and stays benign — a star import still carries only defined globals, but `from helper import Path` now reaches it explicitly.
3. **F24-B is settled by Python's own scoping**, with one rule attached: **a rebind's left-hand side is already prefixed and must not be prefixed again.** Without it `A__count = server__count` inside a function gets re-prefixed and breaks. With it the function-local binding stays local in the bundle exactly as in the source. Same rule answers F19 from the D2 side — a function-local name import is a **binding**, not a use.

## Bloat, measured not estimated

43 imported names across 1551 lines of bundled source — **about +2%**; worst file `dev/xhttp/_/server.py`, 10 imports on 113 lines. Under the alias form non-local imports cost **nothing extra**: the statement is rewritten in place, not supplemented. Bloat falls only on local imports, where the deleted line was going anyway.

add.issue.comment.md:
## Two consequences to carry

- **`EZAVYNM` and `R9H4PVD` are now partly wrong.** `R9H4PVD` is the repair that removes rebinding language from D9 and D19 on the grounds that F13 deleted rebindings. **F13 is reversed. Do not execute either ticket as written** — both need re-deriving against this ruling. `taskupdate #127` carries the same warning.
- **D19's declined warning may be moot.** With every non-local name aliased, three of its four collision sources are structurally prevented rather than merely unlikely. The only survivor is the non-local star import, which D9 already warns about separately. Whether D19 keeps a declined-warning paragraph at all is editorial, not a ruling.

## The bloat, measured

43 imported names across 1551 lines of bundled source — **about +2%**. Worst file `dev/xhttp/_/server.py`, 10 imports on 113 lines. Under the alias form non-local imports cost **nothing extra**: the statement is rewritten in place, not supplemented. Bloat falls only on local imports, where the deleted line was going anyway.

## One shape the alias form cannot express

`import a.b` binds **`a`**, not `a.b`. `import a.b as X` binds `X` to **`a.b`** — a different object. Verified: `import a.b` → binds `['a']`; `import a.b as X` → binds `['X']` where `X` is module `a.b`. So aliasing a dotted module import by rewriting the statement silently rebinds the file to the leaf module and every `a.something` breaks. It needs the two-statement form (`import a.b` + `A__a = a`) or its own rule.

**One occurrence in this repo** — `dev/xhttp/_/helper.py:2`, `import email.utils` — and zero in the released `xlib/`. So this is spec completeness rather than a practical blocker, but it is the one place the ruling does not determine the output and an implementer will meet it. `from . import x` is the other shape named in the same question: it binds `x` from the package, which the alias form expresses directly and which the human's traveller example already assumed works.

add.issue.comment.md:
**RULED, human, 2026-10-15 — the last undetermined output is closed. Dotted module imports use the two-statement form; everything else uses the alias.** Verbatim: *"That solution works for me."*

## The rule

- **`import a.b`** — statement kept verbatim, then one rebind: `import email.utils` · `A__email = email`
- **everything else** — alias in place: `from x import defs as A__defs`, `import math as A__math`, local imports deleted and rebound one per name

So the split is: **the alias rule, except where Python binds a name the statement does not spell.** That is the whole condition — not "dotted imports are different", but "this is the shape where the bound name and the written name differ".

## Verified

The two-statement form, both reaches from one import statement:

```
import email.utils            # kept verbatim, binds `email` unprefixed
A__email = email
A__email.utils.parseaddr(...)          -> ('', 'a@b.com')
A__email.message_from_string(...)       -> 'hi'
```

And the alias form still correct for the shapes it governs: `from os import path as A__path` → `A__path.basename(...)` works.

## Why this needed saying rather than leaving

The failure is half-silent, which is what makes it worth a rule. Applied mechanically, the alias gives the file the **leaf** instead of the **parent**, so `email.utils.parseaddr` keeps working — `email.utils` happens to expose `parseaddr` — while `email.message_from_string` raises `AttributeError: module 'email.utils' has no attribute 'message_from_string'`. A test written against the use that happens to work reports green on a file broken for the other.

It is not fixable by being cleverer with the alias: the parent is unreachable from the child without `sys.modules`. Hence the two-statement form, which is the shape the human preferred originally and which the collision evidence correctly ruled out **for the common case only**. The split is the reconciliation — the cautious form where the cautious form is needed, the cheap form everywhere else.

**One occurrence in this repo** (`dev/xhttp/_/helper.py:2`), zero in released `xlib/`. Spec completeness rather than a blocker.

## Bloat re-measured in bytes, because lines were the wrong unit

The human's correction: *"one needs to think not only of the lines added, but actual filesize. The bundler will in any case end up making names much longer, thus making the whole thing less readable."* Line count hides it, because prefixing lengthens **every reference**, not only the import lines. Counting every load of a module-level global across the 9 bundled files that define any:

| | now | extra | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dev/xhttp/_/err.py` | 832 B | 90 B | **10%** |
| `dev/xconf/xconf.py` | 2 766 B | 210 B | 7% |
| `dev/xschema/xschema.py` | 13 113 B | 819 B | 6% |
| `dev/xcsv/xcsv.py` | 10 932 B | 294 B | 2% |
| **9 files total** | **44 807 B** | **1 618 B** | **+3%** |

The inflation tracks **how many references a module has**, not how many lines or imports it has — `_/server.py` has 10 imports and moves **0%**, `err.py` has 18 references in 832 bytes and moves 10%. This is also before rebind lines are counted, and it flatters XLib: `dev/` is shallow, so prefixes are 4-8 characters. The human's traveller example is the bad case, where `server__ship__` is 13 characters on 4-character names.

Recorded as an accepted cost, not an objection — *"I don't really see a way around it either."*

edit.description.md:
`ctx` gets its rows with `opencode db "$SQL" --format tsv`. opencode 2.0 removed the `db` subcommand entirely (it is absent from `opencode --help` and not under `debug`), so that call now fails and `ctx` dies with `query failed:` plus a dump of the CLI help.

The SQL itself is still correct — the v2 schema keeps the tables and columns `ctx` needs.
